Still, more expansion of exceptions is argued because child and biological father lack standing. If child cannot disavow, personality rights may be seriously infringed or there may be a mismatch between legal and social father-child relationships with no way to correct it.
Legislative policy should grant standing to child and interested parties, but before legislation, interpretation should solve it. One solution is to keep the disavowal route for spouses with standing, and for children without standing allow confirmation action under Article 865 through systematic and rational interpretation.
Courts must interpret statutes harmoniously with constitutional norms. Under current Civil Act, spouses with standing can file disavowal action within 2 years and remove legal parent-child relationship. But the child cannot escape presumption by disavowal action. The Act also has Article 865 confirmation action to correct mismatch between substantive and register parent-child relations. According to Article 865, an interested person may file for nonexistence of natural parent-child relationship on other grounds.
Spouses with disavowal grounds must use disavowal action, so Article 865 cannot be used for the same grounds. But the child, as direct interested party, has no standing for disavowal. If the Act is interpreted to exclude any chance for the child to align legal presumption with biological truth, it seriously restricts child’s rights. Thus it is necessary to see whether Article 865 can remove this irrational result. If ordinary meaning permits the child subject to presumption to file for nonexistence and this does not contradict the purpose of presumption/disavowal provisions, then this interpretation may realize child’s constitutional rights.
First, for the child, although disavowal grounds exist, the child cannot file disavowal action, so Article 865 text does not naturally forbid such claim. But not everyone with an interest can do so. The legislative purpose of restricting disavowal lies in early stability, child welfare, and preventing third-party interference in marital family life. Therefore interested persons who may dispute status should be limited to the extent that legislative purpose is not undermined. The child, as direct interested party, may file confirmation action, but others with status or property interest generally may not unless special circumstances exist.
Even for the child, no unlimited right should exist. Disavowal action has a 2-year filing period. By analogy, the child’s confirmation action should also be limited, with the starting point when the child learned of the cause, or if minor, when reaching majority.
If the child obtains a final judgment of nonexistence, res judicata extends to third parties under family relations registration law, and no one may make contrary claims. But without such judgment, the child cannot immediately deny presumption or file acknowledgment against biological father, and biological father cannot acknowledge the child. Thus it is desirable to solve the standing problem by allowing rebuttal of presumption within the extent that the purpose of the presumption/disavowal system is not nullified.

{"[2018DA1049]": "We consider the grounds for final appeal.

1. Civil Act Article 860은 그 본문에서 “인지 shall have effect retroactively from the time of the child’s birth”라고 하면서, 그 단서에서 “however, it shall not prejudice rights acquired by a third party”라고 하여 인지의 소급효를 제한하고 있고, Civil Act Article 1014는 “if a person who became a co-heir by acknowledgment or by a final and conclusive judgment after the opening of succession claims partition of the inherited property, and another co-heir has already partitioned or otherwise disposed of it, such person has the right to claim payment of an amount equivalent to his/her share of the inheritance”라고 규정하고 있다.
However, 혼인 외의 출생자와 생모 사이에는, 자의 출생으로 생모의 인지나 출생신고를 기다리지 아니하고 법률상의 친자관계가 automatically 생기고 see Supreme Court Judgment 67DA1791, rendered October 4, 1967, 그리고 family relation register의 기재나 법원의 친생자관계존재확인판결이 있어야만 이를 인정할 수 있는 것이 아니다 see Supreme Court Judgment 92NU3199, rendered July 10, 1992. Therefore, Civil Act Article 860의 단서, 즉 인지의 소급효 제한에 관한 규정은 인지를 요하지 아니하는 모자관계에는 apply되지 않고 analogy로도 apply되지 아니하며, 상속개시 후 인지 또는 재판의 확정에 의하여 공동상속인이 된 자의 value payment claim right를 정한 Civil Act Article 1014를 근거로 하여도, 그 자가 모의 다른 공동상속인이 한 상속재산의 분할 또는 처분의 효력을 부인하지 못한다고 볼 수는 없다. This is the same even if, 다른 공동상속인이 이미 상속재산을 partitioned or disposed of 한 이후에, 모자관계가 finality of a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship, etc.에 의하여 비로소 명백히 밝혀졌더라도 마찬가지이다.

2. a. 원심판결 이유에 의하면, the court below determined as follows. 인지 이전에 공동상속인들에 의해 분할되거나 처분된 상속재산은 Civil Act Article 860의 단서가 정한 인지의 소급효 제한에 따라 이를 분할받은 공동상속인이나 양수인에게 확정적으로 귀속되고, this legal principle also applies where, 상속개시 후에 친자관계존재확인의 소의 확정에 의하여 상속인으로 판명된 자가 발생한 경우에도 적용된다. The judgment that a biological parent-child relationship exists between the Plaintiff(selected party) and the designated parties hereinafter referred to as “the Plaintiffs, etc.” and Non-party 1 became final after Defendant 1 disposed of the real property listed in Attached List 1 of the judgment below hereinafter referred to as “the Real Property” to Defendant 2 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership. Ultimately, the Plaintiffs, etc. fall under “a person who became a co-heir by the finality of a judgment after the opening of succession” under Civil Act Article 1014, so they may exercise only the right to claim payment of value equivalent to the purchase price against Defendant 1, and may not deny the effect of the disposition of the Real Property, whose ownership was definitively vested in Defendant 2.

b. However, the above determination by the court below is difficult to accept as it stands for the following reasons.
1) According to the reasons of the judgment below and the record, the following facts can be ascertained.
a) Non-party 1 married Non-party 2 and gave birth to Defendant 1, and thereafter divorced, while maintaining a de facto marital relationship with Non-party 3 and giving birth to the Plaintiffs, etc.
b) Non-party 1 owned the Real Property and died on January 27, 2015. After Defendant 1 completed the registration of transfer of ownership on the Real Property on the grounds of inheritance on June 8, 2015, Defendant 1 sold the Real Property to Defendant 2 on June 25, 2015 and completed the registration of transfer of ownership around that time.
c) On February 12, 2016, the Plaintiffs, etc. filed an action seeking confirmation that a biological parent-child relationship existed between Non-party 1 and the Plaintiffs, etc., and on July 1, 2016, the judgment granting that claim became final and conclusive.
2) In light of the foregoing legal principle, the facts above indicate that between the Plaintiffs, etc. and their birth mother, Non-party 1, a legal parent-child relationship arose automatically by the birth of the Plaintiffs, etc., and it is not the case that such relationship may be recognized only if there is a judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship by a court.
Therefore, Civil Act Article 860의 단서는 the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1 사이에 apply되지 않고 analogy로도 apply되지 않으며, Civil Act Article 1014를 근거로 하여도 the Plaintiffs, etc. may not deny the effect of Defendant 1’s disposition of the Real Property라고 볼 수는 없다. This remains the same even if the judgment confirming the existence of a biological parent-child relationship between the Plaintiffs, etc. and Non-party 1 became final and conclusive only after Defendant 1 had already disposed of the Real Property, thereby making the mother-child relationship clear only then.

c. Nevertheless, the court below, on the grounds set forth above, dismissed the Plaintiffs, etc.’s claim seeking cancellation of the registration of transfer of co-ownership shares in the names of the Defendants with respect to the Real Property, thereby committing an error that affected the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning the establishment of the mother-child relationship and the scope of application of the proviso to Civil Act Article 860 and Article 1014. The allegation in the grounds of final appeal pointing this out has merit.

3. Therefore, without examining the remaining grounds for final appeal, the part of the judgment below against the Plaintiffs, etc. is reversed, and this part of the case is remanded to the court below for further proceedings and determination. It is so decided by the unanimous opinion of the Justices participating in the decision.

{"[2020SEU616]": "We decide the grounds for re-appeal.

1. 사건의 overview and issue
A. 사건의 overview
남성으로 출생한 신청인 겸 사건본인(이하 신청인)은 childhood부터 여성으로의 귀속감을 느꼈고, puberty에 이르러 얼굴, physique, voice가 점점 masculine해지는 것에 mental anguish를 겪었지만 자신의 gender identity를 숨긴 채 혼인하였다가, 약 5년 10개월 후 gender identity 문제로 divorce하였다. 이후 신청인은 2018. 11.경 Thailand의 plastic surgery clinic에서 고환과 음경을 제거하고 female external genitalia의 appearance를 갖추는 surgery를 받았고, thereafter women’s clothes and hairstyle을 하고 사회적으로 woman으로 살아왔다. 신청인은 2012년생 twin 2명의 minor children을 둔 상태에서 family relations register상 gender entry correction permission application, 즉 이 사건 허가 신청을 하였다.
원심은 신청인에게 minor children이 있으므로 gender entry correction을 허가하면 minor children의 welfare에 negative effect가 있다는 이유로 제1심의 dismissal을 upheld하였다.
B. issue in this case
Supreme Court En Banc decision dated 2011. 9. 2., 2009스117 held that in permitting correction of a transsexual person’s gender entry, if the person is currently married or has minor children, correction is not permitted. This case is limited to the latter. In other words, the issue is whether the existence of minor children in the case of a transsexual person who is not presently married should be treated as an independent negative requirement for gender entry correction.

2. 성전환자의 sex determination and family relations register correction
A. The factors determining a person’s sex include not only biological factors such as sex chromosomes and genitalia, but also mental and social factors, such as one’s own sense of belonging to male or female sex and performance of sex roles, namely socially approved behavior, attitude, and personality traits appropriate for a male or female.
In the case of transsexualism, after birth and during growth, such person consistently feels incongruity and aversion toward the birth sex, feels belonging to another sex, and continues to perform roles fitting that other sex. If, under ordinary medical standards, the person can be recognized as not easily assessed as the birth sex, and has reached recognition and acceptance as the transitioned sex in appearance such as genitalia, clothes, hairstyle, and in private and social domains such as sexual relations, friendships, and occupation, then that transsexual person may be legally evaluated as having the transitioned sex, not the birth sex.
B. Supreme Court in 2006. 6. 22. 2004스42 En Banc decision held, based on those legal principles, that in a petition for permission to correct a transsexual person’s gender entry, the sex legally evaluated at present should be reflected in the family register because the register otherwise fails to publicly disclose the current true status relationship. It also held that such permission is a decision confirming the currently true sex newly legally evaluated due to transsexuality, so the effect of the correction does not affect existing status relations or rights and duties.
However, Supreme Court En Banc decision dated 2011. 9. 2., 2009스117 held that where a transsexual person has minor children, the welfare of the minor children must come first, and because correction may cause mental confusion and shock to minor children and expose them to social discrimination or difficulties in daily life through disclosure of family relation certificates, correction is not permitted.

3. Whether permission should be granted for a transsexual person with minor children and the standard
Every human being has the right to form personality according to gender identity and to live life. A transsexual person also should be able to realize personality and individuality based on gender identity and live with others as an equal member of society while pursuing happiness. To fully exercise such rights, the person has the right to have sex according to gender identity legally confirmed as true sex. This is a fundamental right derived from human dignity and value and forms the core of the right to pursue happiness, so it must be guaranteed to the fullest extent.
Meanwhile, a transsexual person with minor children also has the duty as parent to protect and educate the children under Civil Act Articles 913 and 912, so when deciding permission, the court must make a substantive determination by comprehensively considering various circumstances for balance of legal interests in order to harmonize protection of the transsexual person’s fundamental rights with the protection and welfare of minor children. Therefore, one must not deny correction merely because there are minor children without substantive review of those circumstances.
A. About whether to grant permission
1) Protection of fundamental rights such as human dignity and value, and the right to pursue happiness
All citizens have dignity and value as human beings, have the right to pursue happiness, and are equal before the law. Human dignity and value mean that each individual should be respected for unique personality and individuality and should be able freely to choose and develop the content and direction of life deemed most suitable, thereby forming self and destiny. A transsexual person, too, as an equal member of society, has dignity and value as a human being, the right to pursue happiness, and the right to live a human life, and these rights must be protected. So, even in deciding whether to allow gender entry correction, the transsexual person’s fundamental rights must be secured to the fullest extent.
Considering the role that sex distinction and recognition play in society, it is ultimately consistent with social order and public welfare to prevent conflict between actual sex and publicly disclosed sex by allowing public confirmation and disclosure in line with the currently legally evaluated sex. A transsexual person obtaining legal sex publicly through correction does not itself directly harm other members of society. Rather, if the true sex confirmed according to gender identity exists but the sex disclosed through the family relations register does not match it, confusion and misunderstanding among others are likely.
It is correct to regard confirmation of sex in private and public spheres as an essential condition of life for maintaining human dignity, prior to one’s position in the family order. If permission were denied merely because a transsexual person has minor children, then, contrary to the appearance and actual life formed in accordance with gender identity, the person would be shown in official records as pre-transition sex and forced to live an absurd life where actual sex and recorded sex are inconsistent. If such absurdity is forced until the children become adults, the suffering and urgency to confront absurdity would become immense. That result infringes the constitutional demand to respect human dignity and value and to guarantee freedom from discrimination based on gender identity.
Individual family life forms the beginning and core of social relations, and the State must guarantee it under Constitution Article 36(1). A transsexual person, as a family-making member within the overall legal order, should be granted equal rights and duties, and the State must protect those rights.
Although permission may bring change in family relations, that is only a natural process as the rights and duties of a parent are realized differently when one parent’s transsexuality occurs. The parent-child relation and family order thus formed must also be equally respected and protected. This does not change merely because the transsexual person is divorced or not presently married, or because the family relations register has been corrected. The transsexual person with minor children still must exercise rights and perform duties as father or mother, and can do so.
2) Welfare of minor children
It is not correct to uniformly conclude that permission for a transsexual person with minor children itself causes major change in the status relation between parent and child, is manifestly contrary to the children’s welfare, or leaves minor children exposed without protection to social prejudice and discrimination.
Correction simply accepts the actual situation of a transsexual person who has completed transition and reflects it in the record; it does not newly cause major changes in the parent-child status relation or affect the substance of rights and obligations. The personal, social, and legal parent-child relationship does not change before or after correction. Nor can correction itself be viewed as impairing the essential content of the transsexual person’s status and role as father or mother or the children’s rights.
Even if some minor children suffer mental confusion and shock due to a parent’s transsexuality, such confusion arises because the parent has already transitioned, making it an irreversible fait accompli. Correction is a measure to align the official record with the transitioned sex, so it is not right to hastily conclude that permission itself causes mental or psychological shock to minor children.
Likewise, it is wrong to assume adult children can accept it without much confusion but minor children will inevitably suffer such shock. This overlooks the possibility that minor children, with flexible minds, may naturally accept the existence of a transsexual parent.
If emotional and family bonds have already formed between the transsexual person and the children based on the transitioned sex of the father or mother, granting permission is desirable even for the children. Further, even where the children have not yet adapted and are suffering psychological or emotional difficulties, if a divorced transsexual father or mother, through correction, can provide a social and economic foundation to continue raising and supporting the children and an opportunity to seek understanding of transsexuality, that may ultimately serve the children’s welfare by restoring their bond. A transsexual person whose actual sex conflicts with the sex disclosed in the register may have difficulty choosing work suited to appearance or engaging in economic and social activity corresponding to ability and aptitude, and the children may become more unstable and face a poorer environment.
Therefore, without examining the various situations existing or arising between the transitioned parent and the children, the court may fail in substance to act according to the children’s welfare by barring correction merely because there are minor children.
It cannot be concluded that, if permission is granted, minor children will be left unprotected against social discrimination or placed in daily-life difficulties merely because the corrected family relations register may be submitted or disclosed. Even if there is concern over disclosure, the State should protect the children by taking measures to block such disclosure for safeguarding the fundamental rights and privacy of transsexual persons and their minor children; it is not proper to use that concern as a reason to refuse permission.
Our society has long recognized transsexual persons, regardless of correction, by normative assessment based on individual and social recognition, not only biological birth sex. In reality they are minorities, but as neighbors they live ordinary lives and increasingly communicate through mass media by revealing their lives. Understanding has improved, but discrimination and exclusion still exist. If the fact that a transsexual parent’s sex was corrected is disclosed through the family relations register, de facto discrimination may arise for the children. Yet this can be solved by improving the system and procedures and taking measures to prevent disclosure, thereby protecting privacy.
In light of the Constitution’s spirit placing human dignity as the ultimate goal, the State has the duty to prevent unlawful external disclosure of matters related to correction and to make legal and institutional efforts to correct prejudice and misunderstanding against transsexual persons and their families. Refusing permission on those grounds is hard to accept because it abandons the State’s basic duty to prevent harm from social prejudice and to guarantee family stability.
Current Personal Information Protection Act and the Family Relations Registration Act have also improved privacy protection. The present system allows certificates containing only necessary information, lets applicants choose only needed information, restricts persons entitled to request issuance, and has introduced partial certificates. Those who request submission must request the minimum needed information, and use of submitted certificates for other purposes is prohibited. Under the Act, only the person concerned, spouse, parents, or children may inspect the register, and only the person concerned, spouse, or lineal blood relatives may obtain certificates. For a minor child’s family relation certificate, either father or mother may be chosen, and a specific certificate may be issued showing only that parent-child relationship. Also, due to e-government, schools and public institutions process family relation matters without requiring submission or presentation by the party once verified in information systems. In this legal and social reality, careless disclosure to third parties is unlikely.
3) International norms and global trend
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights Article 2 provides that everyone is entitled to all rights and freedoms without distinction such as race, colour, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth, or other status. On 2016. 7. 15., the UN Human Rights Council reaffirmed that all humans are born free and equal in dignity and rights and adopted a resolution opposing violence and discrimination worldwide based on sexual orientation and gender identity; our country voted in favor as a member state.
Also, most countries including Germany, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Sweden, and the United States permit correction for transsexual persons, and most countries except Japan do not treat having minor children as an absolute ground to deny correction. Therefore, denying correction merely because there are minor children runs against international human rights norms and the trend of the world.
B. Standard for determining permission
When deciding whether to allow correction for a transsexual person with minor children, the court must fully guarantee the transsexual person’s constitutional rights such as human dignity and value, the right to pursue happiness, and equality, while keeping in mind the children’s welfare and right to protection and care. So the court should examine not only the general requirements but also the children’s age and physical and mental condition, the degree of their consent or understanding, the form of protection and upbringing, the way the transsexual person performs the parental role, the relationship and bond with children and other family members, and overall family circumstances, and then decide whether granting permission affects the children’s welfare.
In individual cases, the court must closely examine the actual emotional, economic, and social circumstances of the transitioned parent and the children, and make a substantive determination as to which decision protects the transsexual person’s fundamental human rights while also conforming to the children’s welfare, whether disadvantages to the children from permission are markedly greater than restricting the transsexual person’s constitutional rights, and whether refusing permission until adulthood while forcing suffering from mismatch between actual sex and recorded sex is consistent with proportionality. Without such review, uniformly denying permission based on vague concerns may infringe constitutional rights and also harm the substantive welfare of the children.
4. Change of precedent
Therefore, the Supreme Court En Banc decision of 2011. 9. 2., 2009스117, and other decisions to the same effect, are changed to the extent they conflict with this view.
5. Determination in this case
Looking at the court below’s reasoning in light of the above legal principles, the court below cited the 2011. 9. 2. 2009스117 En Banc decision and treated the existence of minor children as an independent negative requirement, and dismissed the application merely because the Applicant has minor children, without specifically examining the record and making a substantive determination. This misapprehends the constitutional principles that all citizens have dignity and value and the right to pursue happiness under Article 10, and that all citizens are equal before the law under Article 11(1), and also misapprehends the criteria for permission while failing to conduct necessary trial. The Applicant’s re-appeal argument is well-founded.
6. Conclusion
Therefore, we reverse the court below and remand for further trial and determination. The participating Justices were unanimous except for Justice Lee Dong-won’s dissent, and there are supplementary opinions by Justices Park Jung-hwa, Noh Jeong-hee, and Lee Heung-gu, and by Justices Kim Seon-su and Oh Kyung-mi.

7. Dissenting opinion of Justice Lee Dong-won
The dissent says that the earlier 2011. 9. 2. 2009스117 En Banc decision held that if a transsexual person has minor children, correction is not permitted. As grounds, it said that under our Civil Act system, in legally evaluating the sex of a person exercising parental authority, the welfare of minor children must come first, and that allowing such permission would significantly affect the special status relation between parent and minor children and the children’s welfare.
The majority appears to view that decision as newly creating the existence of minor children as an independent negative requirement. But before that, in the 2006. 6. 22. 2004스42 En Banc decision, the Court had already presented the basic principle that correction is permitted only if it does not cause a significant change in status relations or negative impact on society and is socially acceptable. The 2011 decision merely clarified that a transsexual person with minor children falls within that contrary case; it did not create a new independent negative requirement.
That decision is consistent with our legal system, the welfare of minor children, and common sense, so it should be maintained. I cannot agree with the majority. The dissent then argues that Constitution Article 36(1) presupposes marriage and family life are founded on the distinction and union of the sexes, and that our Constitution, Civil Act, and statutes presume father is male and mother is female. Therefore, a female father or male mother is not permitted, and granting correction to a transsexual person with children would create a parent-child relationship not permitted under our legal system.
However, a transsexual parent’s correction does not create a new parent-child relationship or status relation not permitted by law. A transsexual parent is still the child’s biological parent and the child remains the transsexual person’s biological child. The parent-child status and rights and duties remain before and after transition. The lack of an adequate term other than father or mother does not mean the original status relation disappears or becomes void. This was already declared in the 2006 decision.
The dissent further says that because the Constitution and Civil Act clearly presuppose father as male and mother as female, correction for a parent with children is not allowed. But language precedes neither nor exhausts human existence; language itself reflects majority order and prejudice. To say that a father becoming female or a mother becoming male is impossible under our legal system is merely to absolutize majority language and deny minority existence. Even if the terms female father or male mother sound unfamiliar, it is wrong to deny the status and rights of transsexual parents and children. Like the word transsexual, language can later be formed to match reality. Thus correction for a transsexual person with children is only a measure to align the already occurred fact of transsexuality with the record; it is not creating a forbidden new status relation.
The dissent also interprets Article 36(1) to mean that the family system is based on gender distinction, but if that is read so strictly it conflicts with Articles 10, 11(1), and 37(1). For protection of the family community, Article 36(1) must be read together with Article 10’s human dignity and pursuit of happiness, Article 10’s duty of the State to confirm and guarantee inviolable fundamental rights, Article 11(1)’s equality, and Article 37(1)’s command that rights not be disregarded because not enumerated. The State must equally protect the family community of a transsexual person and children like any other family. Article 36(1) should be interpreted affirmatively so that a transsexual person with minor children is also protected.
Family community is important, and transsexual persons are no exception. The bond between a transsexual person and family members must be socially respected and legally protected without discrimination. If they wish to cherish that family community and continue living together while maintaining the bond, the State and society must respect that wish and guarantee family life. Modern family communities, including those of transsexual persons, should be accepted and protected within the existing family order to the extent they do not violate social order or public welfare; this strengthens diversity, soundness, and the safety net of society.
In our society, transsexual persons still endure discrimination and exclusion in daily life and law, and suffer the pain of not fully completing their own narrative according to actual gender identity. They are exposed to danger including sexual violence, and this becomes even worse when the sex they disclose does not match the legal sex on IDs or passports. If the light of constitutional human dignity does not reach transsexual minorities equally, its meaning fades. Institutional foundations are needed so transsexual persons may seek life according to true gender identity and discrimination culture be improved. Through that, constitutional guarantees become real, not slogans.
The 2006 decision was the fruit of such efforts. The Court, sympathizing with the hardships transsexual persons endure as a minority, declared that they have the right to request correction according to gender identity as an extension of human dignity and the right to pursue happiness. Correction does not solve everything, but it is an important starting point. To truly solve the difficulties and remedy rights violations, the voices of transsexual persons and families must be reflected through legislation. Yet even after 16 years since that decision, no legal system for transsexual persons has been enacted. In that situation, denying correction again on the ground that legislation is preferable is not proper for a Supreme Court that must protect minorities and their rights until the last moment. Judicial power exists as the last fortress to protect minorities and ensure fundamental rights beyond majority political, religious, and social interests. Courts must not neglect that duty in cases that may infringe human dignity, value, and pursuit of happiness. Even when restriction is thought necessary for order or public welfare, setting an absolute negative requirement is highly risky and must be approached with great caution. The same applies here. Courts must not superficially decide according to majority will without understanding the depth of discrimination and suffering a transsexual person faces. They should exercise pragmatic discretion from a guardianship perspective in line with the nature of non-contentious cases, consider concrete and diverse circumstances, and derive the most reasonable and desirable result. Protecting the rights of transsexual persons, as a minority, and allowing them to live as ordinary neighbors with true gender identity recognized in law is the duty of a court committed to human rights.

8. Supplementary opinion by Justices Park Jung-hwa, Noh Jeong-hee, and Lee Heung-gu
While supplementing the majority opinion, I rebut some dissent arguments as needed.
The dissent says the 2011 En Banc decision should be maintained because it is rational and fits legal system, minor children’s welfare, and social common sense. However, it is hard to accept because it contradicts the purpose of the 2006 En Banc decision, infringes the essential content of a transsexual person’s fundamental rights, and may also run against children’s welfare.
Gender identity is the internal and personal experience and deep sense of belonging a human feels toward gender, regardless of birth sex. Every human beings through gender identity recognize self and complete a personal narrative by reinterpreting and reconstructing experience and giving it meaning. The right concerning gender identity is one of the main contents of the general personality right derived from Constitution Article 10, and has major meaning in existence and life.
A transsexual person is someone whose manifestation of gender identity differs from the biological sex at birth. Human society has divided people into male or female based on birth sex and treated that as unchangeable, while forcing transsexual persons to abandon or conceal their identity. But transsexual persons have long been medically, scientifically, and philosophically confirmed as one form of human existence. The State has a duty to uphold their gender identity rights guaranteed by Article 10.
All citizens have the right to have the sex corresponding to their gender identity indicated consistently in the official record. This is especially important for transsexual persons. If a person with a gender identity different from birth sex is recorded according to biological classification, serious problems arise from inconsistency between reality and public record during transition. Without a procedural right to correct the record, the essential content of the constitutional gender identity right is infringed.
When fundamental rights or public interests conflict, the issue must be resolved by balancing interests under the principle of practical concordance. Restricting correction in the register severely infringes dignity, value, and pursuit of happiness, so serious and clear circumstances showing necessity and lack of alternatives are required. The right to correction can be justified only if harmonized in a way that recognizes the transsexual person’s dignity to the fullest even in relation to minor children.
But under the 2011 decision, courts must deny correction merely because there are minor children, without concrete hearing on what welfare is, what infringement may occur, or whether it is serious and clear. Even when children accept the transsexual parent and live stably while hoping the record be corrected to match reality, the court must deny it. That creates a contradictory situation where the court, which should protect both rights and peaceful lives, infringes both and destabilizes them. It treats children’s welfare abstractly and ignores the concrete meaning of correction in a case like this.
The dissent also narrows the significance of the 2006 decision. The 2006 decision declared as principle that in determining sex, biological and mental-social factors must be comprehensively considered, and if transitioned sex can be recognized, correction must be allowed because the transitioned sex is legally evaluated as that person’s sex. It also stated that the effect of permission or correction does not affect existing status relations or duties. As the supplementary opinion then clarified, the point was not to create a negative requirement that the transsexual person must not change status relations or negatively affect society, but rather that if the person is truly a transsexual person and correction is made accordingly, the effect may be permitted so long as it does not retroactively have a significant effect on existing relations and is limited in scope.
The dissent says the Constitution and our legal system clearly presume father is male and mother is female, so permission for a transsexual parent with children would create an impermissible relationship. But a transsexual parent’s correction does not create a new forbidden parent-child relation. A transsexual parent remains the biological parent and the child remains the biological child. The lack of a proper term other than father or mother does not mean the parent-child rights and duties disappear. Language follows existence, not the other way around. Thus female father or male mother may sound unfamiliar, but that does not make the parent-child relation impermissible.
The dissent again reads Article 36(1) as if it bars correction, but this reading conflicts with Articles 10, 11(1), and 37(1). The family community of transsexual persons and children must be equally protected. Article 36(1) protects family meaning and preciousness based on gender equality and individual dignity, and cannot be used to exclude transsexual family life from protection. It should be interpreted prospectively to include a transsexual person with minor children as a protected subject.
Family community is crucial, and the bond between transsexual persons and family members must be respected and protected. If they cherish the family and wish to continue living together, the State and society must respect that wish and guarantee family life. Accepting and protecting such modern family communities within the existing order, as long as they do not violate social order or public welfare, strengthens social diversity and soundness.
Transsexual persons still live amid discrimination, exclusion, self-division, and threats to existence, and cannot fully complete their narrative according to actual gender identity. They face danger including sexual violence, especially when disclosed sex and legal sex on IDs or passports do not match. If constitutional dignity does not reach them equally, it loses meaning. Institutional foundations are needed so they can live according to true gender identity and discrimination culture can be improved. Then constitutional guarantees become substantive.
The 2006 decision was a result of such efforts. The Court declared that transsexual persons, as equal members of society, have the right to seek correction according to gender identity as part of dignity and pursuit of happiness. Correction is not the solution to everything, but it is an important starting point. To truly solve difficulties, the voices of transsexual persons and families must be reflected through legislation. Yet after 16 years, legislation remains delayed, and denying correction again in the name of legislative preference is not proper. Courts, as the final safeguard of rights, must not abandon minorities. The judiciary should carefully hear the voices of transsexual persons and their families, recognize suffering, and provide a legal environment in which they can live as ordinary neighbors with true gender identity recognized.

9. Supplementary opinion by Justices Kim Seon-su and Oh Kyung-mi
I fully agree with the supplementary opinion of Justices Park Jung-hwa, Noh Jeong-hee, and Lee Heung-gu, and add a few points.
A. The issue of a transsexual person’s gender identity and gender entry correction is a matter of human existence preceding institutions. Therefore, unlike the dissent says, it is not the subject of social pros and cons. Transsexual persons have existed throughout human history, and only recently has their existence been affirmed. From that affirmation, the term transgender also emerged. It is not easy to imagine the suffering and frustration they have borne as a minority. Most people do not experience mismatch between biological sex and internal felt sex, so they rarely face gender identity issues and cannot know the fear and self-denial arising from that gap. Nor can they easily understand the struggle to overcome internal division and form a complete self-image. Because non-transsexual majorities can objectify and observe from the majority’s perspective, these inherent difficulties are intensified by a discriminatory gaze.
B. Modern democratic society values freedom, equality, and respect for human dignity, but institutions and culture are often formed mainly by majority values. As a result, minority voices are buried. The situation of transsexual persons is the same. Social, institutional, and cultural structures treating biological sex as absolute restrict their fundamental rights and tacitly compel them not to reveal themselves. But now we must no longer ignore their cry for equal treatment or leave them in a Homo Sacer state. Correction is essential for them to live according to gender identity. Refusing it denies human existence and drives them to the edge, and also undermines the core values of freedom, equality, and dignity. That is why institutional foundations must be created so they can live here as ordinary neighbors, including through correction.
C. The status of a biological parent as a legal relation transcends the concept premised on father as male or mother as female. It is determined by blood relation through birth, paternity presumption, acknowledgment, and so on, and transsexuality does not change that status or duties. A transsexual person remains someone’s child and remains the biological or legal parent of the child he or she gave birth to. The fact that a parent transitioned does not negate the legally existing parent-child relation or make the child no longer the parent’s biological child.
The dissent says permission for a transsexual parent with children creates a new parent-child relation without legal basis. But human existence precedes the language used to denote it and transcends language. Language reflects majority order and prejudice. To say father becoming female or mother becoming male cannot be permitted is simply to absolutize majority language and deny minority existence. Even if female father or male mother sounds unfamiliar, it is wrong to deny the parent-child status and rights of transsexual persons and their children. Like the word transsexual, language can later be created to fit reality. As the majority opinion and the earlier supplementary opinion said, correction for a transsexual person with children is merely to align the already occurred fact of transsexuality with the record, not to create a forbidden new status relation.
D. Article 36(1) says marriage and family life shall be founded and maintained on individual dignity and equality of the sexes, and the State shall guarantee this. The dissent interprets equality of the sexes as meaning marriage and family are based on sex distinction and union of differentiated sexes, and therefore correction for a transsexual person with children is not permitted. But the 2011 En Banc decision did not expressly say that, nor did it say correction creates a new status relation or changes children’s rights. It reaffirmed the 2006 principle that permission confirms the current true sex newly legally evaluated due to transsexuality, and thus the effect of permission or the correction does not affect existing status relations or duties. It only held that when there are minor children, because social discrimination and prejudice make the negative impact on welfare significant, and because parents must protect children, correction is not permitted where there are minor children.
If Article 36(1) is interpreted as the dissent does, it conflicts with Articles 10, 11(1), and 37(1). For family protection, Article 36(1) must be read with Article 10’s human dignity and pursuit of happiness, the State’s duty to confirm and guarantee inviolable fundamental rights, Article 11(1)’s equality, and Article 37(1)’s command that rights are not disregarded because not enumerated. The State must equally protect the family community of a transsexual person and children like any other family. Article 36(1) should be read prospectively to include that family as a protected subject.
Family community is crucial, and the bond between a transsexual person and family members must be respected and protected without discrimination. If they cherish that family and wish to continue living together, the State and society must respect that wish and guarantee family life. Accepting such modern family communities within the existing order to the extent they do not violate social order and public welfare strengthens diversity, soundness, and the social safety net.
E. In our society, transsexual persons still endure discrimination, exclusion, self-division, and existential threat in daily life and law, and suffer from not being able to complete their narrative according to actual gender identity. Because of appearance or mannerisms, they are easily exposed to danger including sexual violence, especially when their personally disclosed sex does not match the legal sex shown on official documents like IDs and passports.
However noble the constitutional light of human dignity may be, if it does not reach transsexual minorities equally, it fades. Institutional foundations must be laid so they can seek life according to true gender identity, and the culture of discrimination that persists in reality must be improved. Then constitutional dignity and fundamental rights become substantive, not slogans.
The 2006 En Banc decision was the fruit of such efforts. The Court, empathizing with hardships transsexual persons endure as a minority, declared that they have the right to request correction according to gender identity as an extension of dignity and the right to pursue happiness. Correction does not solve everything, but it is an important starting point. Since then, the voices of transsexual persons and families must be reflected through legislation. Yet 16 years later, legislation remains delayed, and transsexual persons still live in the shadow of exclusion. It is necessary to listen to their voices, break the icy silence of rigid order, and sympathize with their suffering. Emphasizing once more the role of the judiciary in protecting the rights of transsexual persons, who are a minority in our society, and the urgency of legislative measures concerning gender entry correction, I state this supplementary opinion to the majority opinion."}

{"[98MEU1698]": "We examine the 상고이유(기간 경과 후에 제출된 상고이유보충서는 상고이유를 보충하는 범위 안에서만 본다).

1. Looking at the 이유 of the 원심판결 in light of the record, the court below lawfully found the following facts by comprehensively considering the evidence it adopted.
(1) 소외 1 met 소외 2, who was operating ○○○호텔 등을 while attending 경희대, around 1958. 5.경, and began dating him; then, after a simple ceremony on the premise of 혼인 secretly from her family and while continuing their 정교관계, she gave birth to 원고 1 on 1959. 6. 10. and to 원고 2 on 1962. 4. 2.
(2) However, since 소외 2의 부모 and others strongly opposed the marriage on the ground that 소외 1의 품행 was not 방정하지 못한 점, 소외 2 had been delaying 혼인신고, but around 1963. he suffered a large loss from 증권투자 and left home around 1963. 4., concealing his 행방 for several months; during that time, on 1963. 9. 3., 소외 1, using 소외 2의 도장 without authorization, filed a 혼인신고 with 소외 2, and also filed 출생신고 for the 원고들 as their 친생자 between them, so that 소외 1 and the 원고들 were each entered in 소외 2의 호적 as his 처 and 자(자).
(3) Accordingly, 소외 2의 어머니 소외 3 filed a 심판청구 with 서울가정법원 against 소외 1 and 소외 2 seeking a ruling confirming that their 혼인 was 무효; meanwhile, 소외 1 filed, with 서울가정법원 65너911호, a 조정신청 against 소외 2 and 소외 3 seeking an order designating 소외 1 as the 양육자 of the 원고들 and requiring them jointly and severally to pay 2,500,000원 as 위자료 because they had made it impossible for her to live together with 소외 2.
Thereafter, when a 판결 confirming the 무효 of the marriage between 소외 2 and 소외 1 was rendered, 소외 1 appealed, then received a 판결 dismissing the appeal, and again filed a 상고, but while the case concerning the claim for 혼인무효확인 was pending before the 대법원, on 1966. 1. 17., in the above 조정사건, a 조정 was 성립 to the effect that the 남녀관계 between 소외 1 and 소외 2 shall be 해소, it shall be confirmed that no 친생자관계 exists between the 원고들 and 소외 2, 소외 1 shall bear all responsibility for the 양육 and other matters concerning the 원고들, 소외 1 shall hereafter be barred from making any and all 재판상 청구 relating to the 원고들, 소외 2 and 소외 3 shall transfer to 소외 1 the 대지 and 건물 located in 서울 중구 장충동, and 소외 1 shall withdraw the 상고 in the case concerning the claim for 혼인무효확인. Pursuant thereto, 소외 1 withdrew the 상고 in the case concerning the claim for 혼인무효확인, the 혼인무효판결 became 확정, and the 원고들 became 혼인외의 자.
(4) On 1967. 6. 1., after the 혼인무효판결 had become 확정, 소외 2 married 피고 보조참가인 1, and between them, gave birth to 피고 보조참가인 2 on 1968. 3. 18. and 피고 보조참가인 3 on 1970. 6. 26., while, against the 원고들, he filed a claim for 인지무효확인 with 서울가정법원 67드877호; in response, 소외 1, in the capacity of the 원고들의 특별대리인, filed with 서울가정법원 68드236호 a 심판청구 against 소외 2 seeking an order designating 소외 4, the 원고들의 외조모, as the 양육자 of the 원고들 and requiring payment of the 양육비.
Accordingly, on 1968. 9. 6., a 심판 was rendered confirming that the 인지(출생신고) made by 소외 2 to the 종로구청장, 서울특별시, as of 1963. 9. 3., identifying the 원고들 as his 자(자), is 무효. In the case concerning the 양육자지정 등 청구 filed by 소외 1 on behalf of the 원고들, on 1968. 9. 19., a 재판상 화해 was 성립 to the effect that the 원고들이 are not the 친생자 of 소외 2, 소외 2 shall pay 3,500,000원 to the 원고들, and the 원고들 shall make no further 금원청구. And as the 심판 confirming 인지무효 became 확정, the 원고들 were removed from 소외 2의 호적, and by 일가창립, each was entered as 호주, with the 부란 left blank and the 모 designated as 소외 1.
(5) After the above 재판상 화해 had been 성립, 소외 1 married another man and cut off relations with the 원고들; meanwhile, 소외 2, while substantially performing the role of the 원고들의 아버지 by, inter alia, giving them 학비 so that they could study abroad and attending their weddings, died on 1994. 11. 30., and the 원고들 filed the instant 인지청구 on 1995. 1. 4.
2. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the 본안전 항변 portion
The court below, in response to the 참가인들의 assertion that the instant 인지청구 conflicts with the 기판력 of the final and conclusive 심판 confirming 인지무효 and of the 조정 and 재판상 화해 that included confirmation that no 친생자관계 exists between the 원고들 and 소외 2, and that it also violates the 금반언의 원칙 in light of the contents of that 조정 and 재판상 화해, and further constitutes an abuse of 권리 as the exercise of a 소권 that had already ceased after 사실상 waiver or 소멸 of the 인지청구권, held that the final and conclusive 심판 confirming 인지무효 clearly had as its 심판대상 a confirmation that the 임의인지 by 출생신고 was 무효 because, despite the fact that 소외 2 himself had never acknowledged the 원고들 as his 친생자 or filed their 출생신고, the 호적 was entered as if such act had been done by 소외 1; accordingly, its 기판력 arises only to the extent that the 임의인지 by 출생신고 of 소외 2 is 무효, and its effect does not extend even to whether a 친생자관계 exists between 소외 2 and the 원고들; therefore, the effect of that final and conclusive 심판 does not extend to the instant claim seeking 재판상 인지 on the premise that a 친생자관계 exists between the 원고들 and 소외 2, and a claim concerning the 존부확인 of a 친생자관계, which corresponds to a 가류 가사소송사건 under the current 가사소송법, by its nature concerns matters over which the parties cannot freely 처분, and thus even if 조정 or 재판상 화해 is 성립 thereon, it cannot have legal effect (see 대법원 1968. 4. 6. 선고 65다139, 140 판결); therefore, the above 조정 or 재판상 화해 has no effect with respect to confirming that no 친생자관계 exists between the 원고들 and 소외 2, and there is no room for 기판력 to arise, and moreover, the 인지청구권 cannot be 포기, and even if 포기하였다 하더라도 no effect can arise (see 대법원 1987. 1. 20. 선고 85므70 판결), so it cannot be said that the 원고들이 waived their 인지청구권 or forfeited it due to the 조정 or 재판상 화해, and thus the instant claim cannot be said to violate the 금반언의 원칙 or to constitute 권리남용, and accordingly rejected all of the 참가인들의 arguments.
Examining the record, the above determination by the court below is correct, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as misapprehension of the law concerning 기판력, 쟁점효, 권리실효, 권리포기, or the 금반언의 원칙. The grounds of appeal on this point cannot be accepted.
3. Regarding the grounds of appeal on the merits
According to the reasons of the judgment below, the court below, on the basis of the commissioned 유전자감정 results and 사실조회 results among the evidence it adopted, found that the possibility that 망 소외 2 was the biological father of the 원고들 could not be ruled out, and that the 부권확률 was, in the case of 원고 2, as low as 88.029% and as high as 99.9999999998%, and, in the case of 원고 2, as low as 91.891% and as high as 99.99999999995%; then, comprehensively considering the factual circumstances noted above, it recognized that the 원고들 were the 친생자 of 망 소외 2 born between 소외 1 and 망 소외 2, and granted all of the 원고들의 claims for 인지 in this case.
Comparing the relevant evidence with the record, such factual findings by the court below are acceptable, and it cannot be said that there is any illegality such as violation of the 채증법칙, factual error due to insufficient 심리, 판단유탈, or misapprehension of the law concerning the 입증책임. The grounds of appeal on this point are likewise not accepted.
4. Therefore, all appeals are dismissed, and the costs of appeal shall be borne by the 패소자들. The judgment is rendered as per the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding 주관적 범죄성립요건 is correct? (Where there is a dispute, according to 판례)
A: With 살의를, if the actor assaults the victim (act (a)), and when the victim loses consciousness and goes limp, mistakenly believes the victim to be dead and buries the victim in sand for the purpose of 증거 인멸 (act (b)), and it is found that the victim died from act (b), since the 직접 원인 of death is act (b), attempted murder is established.
B: In order for an actor’s conduct to qualify as 긴급피난, it is sufficient that the actor has only 인식 of the 긴급피난상황; an intent to 피난 the 위험 is not also required.
C: Where a person, with the purpose of 모해, instigates a person who does not have the purpose of 모해 to commit 위증, under the principle of 공범종속성, the offense of 위증교사, rather than 모해위증교사, is established.
D: If a witness, being 착오, testifies to content contrary to 객관적 사실 without awareness that it is contrary to his or her own 기억, intent to commit 위증 can be recognized.
E: Where an actor who accidentally received a 착오송금 from a trading company that is in litigation over a claim for payment of the price of goods refuses to return the mistakenly remitted money with the intent to exercise a lawful right of 상계 against the price of the goods, the establishment of 불법영득의사, which is an element of 횡령, may be denied.

{"[2021DO2088]": "상고이유를 판단한다.

1. 공소사실 요지  
이 사건 공소사실의 gist는 다음과 같다.  
The Defendant는 주류회사인 B Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “B”)의 inside director로서, Victim과 주류 supply 거래를 해오던 사람이었다. The Defendant는 Victim을 상대로 주류대금 지급을 구하는 civil action을 제기하여 civil dispute 중인 2019. 9. 30. Victim으로부터 Defendant가 관리하는 B 명의 account로 4,700,000원을 remitted받아 보관하게 되었다. However, the above amount was money that the Victim had intended to remit to Co., Ltd. C이고, account number 착오로 Defendant에게 remitted된 것이었으며, The Defendant는 2019. 10. 1. Victim으로부터 위 금원이 mistaken remittance된 것이라는 사실을 text message로 통지받아 위 금원을 return해야 할 의무가 있었다. Nevertheless, The Defendant는 Victim과 set-off and settlement에 관한 agreement 없이, Defendant가 주장하는 주류대금 claim amount인 1,108,310원을 unilateral하게 set off and settle한 뒤 return을 refused하여 embezzled하였다.

2. 원심판단  
The court below held that, with respect to the money mistakenly remitted by the Victim to the Defendant, so long as a 신의칙상 custodial relationship is 인정되는 이상, 목적이나 용도를 한정하여 entrusted된 money와 마찬가지로 The Defendant가 unilateral하게 set off할 수는 없다고 보아, The Defendant의 act는 횡령죄의 요소인 “반환의 거부”에 해당하고 불법영득의사도 인정된다는 이유로 이 사건 공소사실을 guilty로 판단하였다.

3. 대법원의 판단  
a. 형법 제355조 제1항에서 정하는 “반환의 거부”란 보관물에 대하여 owner의 rights를 배제하는 intention 표시를 하는 act를 뜻하므로, “반환의 거부”가 횡령죄를 구성하려면 타인의 재물을 보관하는 자가 단순히 return을 refused한 사실만으로는 부족하고, 반환거부의 reason과 subjective intentions를 종합하여 그 반환거부행위가 횡령행위와 같다고 볼 수 있을 정도여야 한다. 횡령죄에서 불법영득의사란 타인의 재물을 보관하는 자가 그 취지에 반하여 정당한 권원 없이 스스로 owner처럼 이를 dispose하려는 intention을 말하므로, 비록 return을 refused하였더라도 반환거부에 정당한 reason이 있다면 불법영득의사가 있다고 할 수 없다(대법원 1998. 7. 10. 선고 98도126 판결, 대법원 2002. 9. 4. 선고 2000도637 판결, 대법원 2015. 2. 26. 선고 2014도11552 판결 등 참조).

b. 원심판결 reasons와 record로 알 수 있는 다음 circumstances를 이러한 legal principles에 비추어 살펴보면, 피고인이 피해자의 착오로 B 명의 account로 remitted된 금전 중 B의 피해자에 대한 claim amount에 상응하는 부분에 관하여 반환을 refused한 행위는 valid한 set-off right의 exercise로 볼 여지가 있으므로, 피고인의 반환거부행위가 횡령행위와 같다고 보고 불법영득의사를 인정한 원심의 determination은 그대로 받아들이기 어렵다.

(1) 어떤 deposit account에 money가 mistake로 잘못 remitted되어 deposited된 경우 수취인과 송금인 사이에 신의칙상 custodial relationship은 성립하지만(대법원 2010. 12. 9. 선고 2010도891 판결, 대법원 2018. 7. 19. 선고 2017도17494 전원합의체 판결 등 참조), 특별한 circumstances가 없는 한 이러한 이유만으로 송금인이 mistaken remittance한 money가 위탁자가 purpose와 use를 정하여 expressly entrusted한 money와 identical하다거나, 송금인이 수취인에게 money의 receipt and payment를 수반하는 affairs 처리를 entrusted하였다고 보아 수취인의 송금인에 대한 set-off right exercise가 original entrustment 취지에 반한다고 평가할 수는 없다.

(2) related civil case의 진행경과에 비추어 보면 B는 이 사건 공소사실 기재 반환거부 시점경 피해자에 대하여 반환거부 금액에 상응하는 물품대금채권을 보유하고 있었던 것으로 보인다. 그 당시 B의 위 물품대금채권과 피해자의 부당이득반환채권이 서로 set-offable relation에 있지 않았다거나, B의 set-off right exercise가 신의칙 위반이나 right abuse에 해당한다고 볼 만한 material이나 circumstances도 보이지 않는다.

(3) The Defendant는 착오송금된 4,700,000원 중 B의 위 물품대금채권액 1,108,310원에 상응하는 금액을 제외한 remainder는 송금 다음날 반환하였고, 1,108,310원에 대해서도 반환을 request한 Victim에게 B의 위 물품대금채권을 automatic claim으로 하여 set-off right를 exercise하겠다는 intention을 충분히 밝힌 것으로 보인다. In this manner, The Defendant가 위 물품대금채권액에 상응하는 money에 대한 return을 refused한 reason과 subjective intention을 살펴보면, The Defendant가 불법영득의사를 가지고 return을 refused한 것이라고 단정하기 어렵다.

c. 그런데도 원심은 The Defendant의 반환거부행위를 횡령죄에서의 embezzlement act와 같다고 보고 불법영득의사를 인정하여 위 공소사실을 guilty로 판단하였다. The judgment of the court below에는 횡령죄에서의 embezzlement act 및 불법영득의사에 관한 법리를 오해하여 필요한 심리를 다하지 않음으로써 judgment에 영향을 미친 error가 있다.

4. 결론  
The judgment of the court below is reversed, and the case is remanded to the court below for further trial and determination. It is so adjudged in accordance with the unanimous opinion of the participating Justices, as stated in the disposition."}
