Section 1. 공소 기각의 결정을 간과한 위법

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, even based on the facts stated in the indictment, there is no statement of specific facts concerning the purpose of 국헌문란, the 폭동 acts, and the contents of the conspiracy, which are constituent elements of the crime of 내란, or concerning the division of execution in the co-principal offense of murder; thus, because the facts charged are not specified, an order dismissing the prosecution should have been entered pursuant to Article 373(1)4 of the Military Court-Martial Act, but the lower court overlooked this and thereby erred in misunderstanding the above legal principles. We shall first consider this point.

Upon review, this point was already lawfully considered by the lower court. In addition, the facts charged against the Defendants, as organized from the indictment in this case and the applications to amend the indictment made on two occasions, are sufficiently specified on their face to be recognized as the relevant offenses, and it is admitted that they are specifically stated. Further, as to the murder of Defendant C, the indictment clearly charges co-principal liability by conspiracy; accordingly, in that case, the omission of facts concerning the division of execution in co-principal liability cannot be deemed a defect. Therefore, this argument is without merit.

Section 2. procedural 위법

1. Violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that, according to the indictment and the application to amend the indictment, Defendant G was prosecuted for killing T and U with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, but the lower judgment found Defendant G to have killed six persons, namely B, T, V, W, X, and U; this, it is argued, is a violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication and thus a violation of law. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the application to amend the indictment lawfully granted at the first trial date in the lower court (trial transcript p. 1458), it is clear, as argued, that Defendant G was prosecuted for having killed T and U, among the six deceased persons in this case, for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. However, in the reasoning of the lower judgment, in the conclusion portion concerning the facts of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose, the court stated: “From around 19:40 to 20:05 on the same day, former President B, ..., the said T, ..., the said V, ..., the said W, the said X, and the said U were each caused to die, thereby the Defendants jointly murdered the above victims for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.” This appears, on its face, to have committed the illegality alleged. Nevertheless, the lower court had previously stated that, on October 26, 1979, around 19:40, Defendant G, after the other Defendants had fired at the above deceased persons, received at around 20:05 that day an instruction from Defendant E to carry out a confirmation shot on persons not yet fully dead and agreed to participate in that killing. Not only that, but the lower court also stated that, with respect to the shooting pursuant to that instruction, it was done by firing “one shot at the said W lying fallen, two shots at the said V, two shots at the said T groaning, and one shot at the said U lying fallen and groaning.” In view of this point, although the expression in the conclusion portion of the lower judgment is somewhat inaccurate, it is still recognized that the lower court judged within the scope of the prosecution. The argument is without merit.

2. Violation of “public trial”

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the court-martial of first instance, at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, conducted the defense counsel’s statements and questioning of Defendant A in closed session without satisfying the prescribed requirements, and also, at the ninth trial date on December 18, 1979, effectively prohibited public access and proceeded with Defendant A’s final statement without even entering a decision of closure; thus, it is argued that the closed proceedings were plainly illegal in their grounds and procedure. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the record (trial transcript p. 223), at the second trial date on December 8, 1979, during the defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A, the court ordered a closed proceeding on the ground that “Defendant A, as former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, has performed important duties concerning foreign intelligence and domestic security intelligence, security affairs pertaining to state secrets, insurrection, foreign relations, the investigation of crimes prescribed in the National Security Act, the Anti-Communist Act, and similar laws, and the coordination and supervision of intelligence and security affairs, and the content of the defendant’s statements in this court pursuant to the defense counsel’s cross-examination substantially includes matters that may interfere with the security or public order of the State.” It then proceeded in camera thereafter. This was based on Article 67 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that “the oral proceedings and judgment in trial shall be public; provided, however, that where public order may be disturbed, morals harmed, or where necessary for military secrecy, the military court may decide not to hold them publicly.” Even in light of the record, the reason is fully understandable. Therefore, the first-instance court’s measure was proper and cannot be said to have been mistaken. Accordingly, this portion of the argument is without merit.

Further, whether any stage of the trial proceedings was public is to be recorded in the trial transcript pursuant to Article 85(2)5 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which prescribes the entries in the trial transcript. Article 89 of the same Act provides that “matters recorded in the trial transcript as procedural acts on a trial date are proved by that transcript alone.” Thus, the public or private nature of the proceedings on December 18, 1979, the ninth trial date in the first instance, can be established only by the trial transcript in this case. The first-instance ninth trial transcript (trial transcript p. 769) states in the column for “public or private” that the trial was “public in court.” Therefore, it can be recognized that the proceedings on that date were conducted in a public courtroom. Accordingly, this argument also lacks merit.

3. Illegality of limiting examination

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the lower court, though under Article 344 of the Military Court-Martial Act they could limit examination only to the extent that the essential rights of parties to the litigation were not harmed, nevertheless restricted examination and statements whenever specific references were to be made in the course of examining Defendant A concerning the motive and purpose of this act, the domestic political situation immediately before the act, and the inevitability of the act, and also frequently imposed limitations during the examination of Defendants E and F; this, it is argued, constituted a grave infringement of the Defendants’ and counsel’s right of defense beyond the permissible bounds of examination restriction. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts, it can be recognized that the first instance and the lower court afforded the above Defendants necessary and sufficient opportunities to make statements, and that each defense counsel was granted the necessary right to examine the Defendants and other parties to the litigation; further, it is sufficiently recognized that each defense counsel had necessary and sufficient opportunities to defend the Defendants, which were realized, and that each Defendant had a full opportunity to make final statements. In particular, in the case of Defendant A, from the content of the Defendant’s statements in response to examinations by the prosecutor, defense counsel, and legal officer in the first-instance and appellate courts, as well as the supplemental statement of reasons for appeal submitted by Defendant A himself (trial transcript p. 1695), and the statements of reasons for appeal and grounds of appeal submitted by his counsel, it can be recognized that the defense content alleged by the appellant is sufficiently reflected. Therefore, the contrary argument lacks merit.

4. Illegality of ordering withdrawal from the courtroom

Among the grounds of appeal, when questioning Defendant C and others at the third trial date on December 10, 1979, the first-instance court, invoking Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, ordered Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that he could not make sufficient statements in Defendant A’s presence; this, it is argued, was done without just cause solely upon the application of the prosecutor, and furthermore, when Defendant C’s statement ended in that case, Defendant A, who had been withdrawn, should have been brought back into the courtroom and informed of the substance, and Defendant A should have been allowed to question Defendant C directly, but instead the proceedings were simply closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom that day; this is said to be illegal. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the first-instance third trial transcript, before the examination of Defendant C at the said third trial date, the first-instance court, ex officio, ordered the remaining Defendants including Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that they were deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of co-defendants (trial transcript p. 237). This measure was based on Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that “the presiding judge may order the defendant to withdraw and be questioned when, on his own motion or upon application by the prosecutor, the defendant is deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of another defendant or ....” In light of the record, this was reasonable. It is true, as argued, that after Defendant C’s statement ended at that date, the proceedings were closed without Defendant A being brought back into the courtroom. However, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, when the first-instance court resumed and, at the fourth trial date, the legal officer informed the parties in the courtroom, which included all defendants in this case including Defendant A and all their counsel, of the substance of the previous court hearing on Defendant C, and asked the parties for their views, the parties stated that they had no particular opinion; this is clearly shown in the record (trial transcript p. 318). Further, according to the first-instance sixth trial transcript, it is clearly shown in the record that Defendant A’s assigned counsel O and Y cross-examined Defendant C on behalf of Defendant A (trial transcript pp. 518, 520). Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

5. Illegality in witness examination procedure

Among the grounds of appeal, first, according to the witness examination record of Z adopted by the lower court, it is clear that Defendant A was not allowed to participate in the examination of that witness. This, it is argued, violated the law guaranteeing a defendant’s right to participate in witness examination and, through that, the right of cross-examination. Second, it is argued that, in examining witnesses, there was no service of summons by the prescribed procedure under Articles 106 through 108 of the Military Court-Martial Act; moreover, in some cases, witnesses were made to wait in advance before the prosecutor had even applied for evidence, and then were taken up and examined immediately upon application; this, it is argued, was not only a procedural violation but a grave illegality depriving the Defendants and their counsel of the opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We consider this argument.

Upon review, first, according to the first-instance trial record, at the eighth trial date at which all the Defendants in this case and their counsel were present, regarding witness Z who failed to appear, the first-instance court instructed the legal officer that he would conduct the examination outside the courtroom and ordered the attendance of the relevant persons (trial transcript p. 707). Thereafter, on December 17, 1979, legal officer AA examined the witness at the Army Headquarters Judge Advocate General’s Office, where Defendant C and his counsel and the counsel for Defendants A and D were present (trial transcript p. 749). In the manner of that witness examination, it cannot be said that Defendant A was not notified and thus was denied an opportunity to participate. Moreover, the witness’s testimony primarily concerned the criminal facts of Defendant C, so it cannot be said that there was any illegality in the procedure. In addition, according to the same trial record, at the ninth trial date resumed on December 18, 1979, the first-instance court, after the legal officer informed the courtroom that witness Z had been examined, presented the substance and asked the parties for their opinions; the parties stated that they had no particular opinion, as clearly shown in the record (trial transcript p. 771). Therefore, even if there were a mistake as alleged, the Defendants and their counsel stated at the evidence examination that they had no particular opinion, so the mistake would be cured by waiver of the right to object (see Supreme Court decisions dated May 20, 1962, 4294HYEONGSANG127; July 4, 1967, 67DO613; and April 8, 1975, 74DA3323). Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.

Second, according to the first-instance trial record, after the first-instance court selected eight witnesses at the sixth trial date, it examined the two selected witnesses who appeared at the seventh trial date (trial transcript p. 571), and at the eighth trial date it newly selected nine witnesses present at the court and examined those witnesses and the five witnesses selected earlier who appeared (trial transcript p. 629). Also, one witness examination was conducted outside the courtroom by legal officer AA on December 17, 1979, all of which is clear from the relevant trial transcripts and witness examination records. Under the proviso of Article 192 of the Military Court-Martial Act, witnesses present in court may be examined without summons, so it cannot be illegal that the nine present witnesses were not summoned. Nor can it necessarily be faulted that those witnesses were examined immediately upon application. As to the remaining witnesses, although summons procedures should have been taken, no trace of the issuance of summons can be found in the record (except that the trial transcripts state that they were summoned and appeared). However, after examining those witnesses and the witness outside the courtroom, the first-instance court afforded the Defendants and their counsel the opportunity to state their opinions in court or at the next trial date, and they stated that they had no particular opinion. Moreover, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendants and their counsel conducted sufficient and necessary cross-examination of those witnesses. Therefore, the defect of non-issuance of summons cannot be said to be a case affecting the outcome of the judgment, and this portion of the argument also cannot be accepted.

6. Illegality in opening the proceedings without counsel

Among the grounds of appeal, in military court cases, counsel is mandatory under Articles 62 and 315 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and therefore proceedings cannot be opened without counsel’s appearance. Nevertheless, on January 22, 1980, at the first trial date, as a measure under Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act rather than severance of trial, the lower court opened proceedings with only Defendants C and G present and without the appearance of Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel, and is alleged to have illegally examined matters concerning the motives and circumstances of the co-defendants’ offenses. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the appellate trial record, after notifying Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel that the first trial date was set for January 22, 1980 (trial transcript pp. 1007, 1009-1011, 1019-1021, 1024, 1040-1044), the court later re-designated and notified the trial date as January 23, 1980 (trial transcript p. 1381). Then, at the first trial date on January 22, 1980, the court, pursuant to Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act, deemed that some of the Defendants including Defendants A, E, and F need not appear at trial and did not order their appearance, but proceeded with the hearing with only Defendants C and G present (trial transcript p. 1383). Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act is only the provision that in appellate proceedings under the Military Court-Martial Act, the appeal instance is not a de novo trial of the first instance, but rather a post hoc review of specific factual and legal issues in the first-instance judgment, and thus as a rule the defendant need not appear at appellate trial dates. It is not a provision allowing only some co-defendants to appear selectively, as in this case, and excusing the appearance of the others. Therefore, the above measure of the appellate court was mistaken. However, at the continued second trial date on January 23, 1980, the legal officer informed the substance of the important matters of the previous trial hearing (trial transcript p. 1469), and thereafter sufficient opportunity for cross-examination was afforded. Moreover, the record shows that the first instance had already conducted sufficient hearings on the matters alleged in the appeal grounds, and at the first appellate trial date there is no indication that new matters were examined on that point. Accordingly, the error was not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. The Supreme Court decisions cited by the appellant are not apt to this case. Thus, this argument also cannot be accepted.

7. Deprivation of the right to counsel

Among the grounds of appeal, the Defendants’ lineal family members and spouse have, under Article 59 of the Military Court-Martial Act, an independent right to appoint counsel. Thus, even if the defendant himself refuses to argue, the right of counsel appointed by the lineal family members and spouse does not extinguish. Nevertheless, counsel AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s lineal family members and spouse were denied entry into the courtroom by military police serving as courtroom order personnel pursuant to the judge’s order at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, and it is argued that thereby their right to counsel was deprived, and that the court committed illegality in failing to decide on the objection to this point. We consider this argument.

Upon review, even if, pursuant to Article 59(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, the defendant’s lineal family members and spouse may independently appoint counsel, the appointing party is one who independently exercises the appointing right of the principal, so the effect of the appointment extends to the principal, and the principal must be understood as being able to revoke the appointment. In this case, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, while the hearing at the fourth trial date proceeded under the participation of privately retained counsel including attorneys AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s mother and spouse, Defendant A stated, “From now on, I refuse the defense by the private defense team for this defendant.” At that time the legal officer informed him of the fact that “the military court requires counsel and, if the privately retained counsel must be dismissed, the military court must decide to appoint assigned counsel.” Defendant A then stated, “Please appoint assigned counsel for this defendant; I will revoke all privately retained counsel for myself.” This is clearly shown in the record (trial transcript pp. 346-347). Therefore, the above private counsel were lawfully revoked, and the fact that they were later denied entry to the courtroom as counsel at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, cannot be regarded as deprivation of the right to counsel. Nor can it be said that any illegality occurred merely because the objection thereto was not decided. The argument is without merit.

8. Deficiency in the trial transcript and deprivation of the rights of inspection and copying

Among the grounds of appeal, even if the Military Court-Martial Act does not have a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act that trial transcripts must be promptly prepared within five days after each trial date, considering Articles 89 (probative force of the trial transcript), 86 (special provisions concerning the trial transcript), and 64 (inspection and copying of documents and evidence), etc., the trial transcript in military court proceedings should also be prepared before the next trial date or, at the latest, before the factual hearing ends. Nevertheless, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court did not promptly prepare the trial transcripts, thereby effectively depriving counsel of the right under Article 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act to inspect and copy the transcripts, etc. We consider this argument.

Upon review, the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which sets a statutory period for preparing trial transcripts. Of course, military court trial transcripts must also be prepared promptly, but one cannot definitively say by when they must be completed. In particular, even the statutory period set by the Criminal Procedure Act is only a directive provision, and merely failing to complete the transcript within that period cannot by itself be regarded as rendering the trial transcript void. Therefore, no fault can be found with respect to the timing of preparation of the first-instance and appellate trial transcripts; nor can it be said that there was illegality in depriving the right of inspection and copying of transcripts. The gist of the argument is that it concerns the defendants’ right of defense. Upon review of the first-instance and appellate trial records in this case, it is recognized that the defendants’ right of defense was fully protected; accordingly, this argument cannot be accepted.

9. Infringement of the independence of the trial

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the first instance and appellate court pressed ahead with the hearing as though there were a fixed, predetermined schedule under the aforementioned unlawful procedures infringing the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel, and that even during the hearing, there were cases in which notes of contact from outside were publicly and repeatedly handed to the judges through the back door behind the judges’ bench; this, it is argued, violated Article 102 of the Constitution and Article 28 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which guarantee judicial independence. We consider this argument.

As to the arguments alleging that the above first-instance and appellate trial procedures were illegal, we have already found them to be without merit. Even in light of the record, it is not recognized that the factual hearings in the first instance and appellate court were pressed ahead under some fixed schedule as alleged. Rather, the record only shows that the first instance conducted sufficient factual hearings eight times across the second through ninth trial dates, and the appellate court did so three times across the first through third trial dates, while ensuring the defendants’ right of defense and right to counsel. No other illegality is found. Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing in the record suggesting that contact notes were delivered to the judges during the hearing, and especially whether their content infringed judicial independence is wholly unknown. This point is too abstract and fabricated to require further discussion. Therefore, the argument lacks merit.

Section 3. 검찰관작성의 피의자신문조서에 대한 「임의성」 issue

Among the grounds of appeal, it is argued that the suspect-interrogation records concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were merely an extension of the records prepared by the military police investigators because, at the time of the prosecutor’s interrogation, the Defendants were physically and mentally exhausted by numerous acts of torture at the joint investigation headquarters under martial law, and in particular Defendant A made statements involuntarily, under the prosecutor’s earnest persuasion, while his consciousness was dim due to aggravation of his chronic liver disease; or because the prosecutor conducted the interrogation at the place where the military judicial police had investigated after receiving the case, under a state in which access and communication with counsel and family were completely prohibited, and the record content was the same as the military judicial police records except for legal refinement, so that it lacked “voluntariness.” It is argued that the lower court nevertheless used this as evidence of guilt, thereby committing an error of law concerning evidentiary capacity or a defect for failure to provide reasons, and also erred by omitting consideration of the grounds of appeal. We consider this argument. (This point is related to the argument below that the fact-finding violated the rules of evidence, and for convenience it is considered separately.)

Upon review, in general, the absence of voluntariness in a statement means that the person being interrogated by an investigative authority did not make the statement under free conditions because of threats, torture, or other means. The determination of voluntariness is made within a reasonable scope by the free conviction of the judge without violating the rules of experience. It suffices that the adjudicating panel makes a reasonable judgment in all respects of the litigation process—namely, the preparation and content of the document, the defendant’s explanation and demeanor, the prosecutor’s elucidations, and the testimony of witnesses involved in the preparation of the document. On that basis, the record shows the following:

(1) In the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the second trial date in the first instance:
Q: “When the prosecutor investigated, I wrote the record and made you verify it item by item, did I not?”
A: “Yes.”
Q: “After confirming the contents, you signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 210)

(2) During the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A at the third trial date in the first instance:
Q: “During the prosecutor’s investigation, was there any instance in which you made a statement under compulsion or threat?”
A: “I said, please write it as it was.”
(Trial transcript p. 247)
And:
Q: “When the prosecutor investigated, was there any threat or coercion?”
A: “No.”
Q: “You reviewed the record prepared at that time, confirmed the contents, and signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 256)

(3) During the cross-examination of Defendant A by defense counsel AC at the first appellate trial date:
Q: “Looking at the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation record concerning the defendant, it says that during a conversation at the curb in front of the entrance you nodded your head and thought you would kill T, and where was that record prepared?”
A: “I do not know the exact location, but the prosecutor came to the Joint Investigation Headquarters and took the record for two days.”
Q: “Was there no investigation at the Prosecutor’s Office?”
A: “There was. After that, they came to the Judge Advocate General’s Office twice and investigated me.”
Q: “Then, did the prosecutor investigate you on the spot immediately after the Joint Investigation Headquarters investigation?”
A: “No. After the case was transferred to the Prosecutor’s Office, the prosecutor came to that place and investigated me.”
Q: “At that time, did you clearly know that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor?”
A: “I clearly knew that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor and that he was a military prosecutor.”
(Trial transcript pp. 1398-1400)

(4) During the cross-examination of Defendant F by his counsel Y at the fifth trial date in the first instance:
Q: “When you were investigated before the prosecutor, did you tell the truth and read the contents?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 430)

(5) During the cross-examination of Defendant G by his counsel P at the same trial date:
Q: “Did the prosecutor write the record as you said?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 435)

(6) Through the hearings in the first instance and appellate court, there is no statement to be found that the Defendants were investigated under a non-free atmosphere such as assault or deception during the prosecutor’s interrogation of suspects.

(7) According to the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records for the Defendants, the statements of the Defendants are almost identical in content concerning the circumstances and details of the offense in this case, with only some differences in expression, and in particular, as for Defendants C, D, E, and G, they were investigated on two occasions and the statements on both occasions are consistent.

(8) In the trial hearings in the first instance and appellate court as well, the Defendants’ statements in court are largely the same as the contents of the prosecutor’s statements regarding objective facts, differing only as to some subjective matters such as motive, and this becomes even more pronounced as the proceedings progress. These facts are apparent from the record. Taking these together with other circumstances appearing in the record, the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records for the Defendants are all admitted to have voluntariness. Therefore, the lower court’s use of them as evidence of guilt was proper, and there is no illegality as alleged. Accordingly, this part of the argument lacks merit.

And although Defendant C’s counsel AC raised this point in the statement of grounds of appeal submitted, the lower court’s failure to decide it was mistaken (trial transcript p. 1128); however, since the argument is plainly without merit as above, the mistake could not have affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, this point also lacks merit.

Section 4. 범죄구성요건에 관한 위법

1. Purpose of “국헌문란”

Among the grounds of appeal, the “국헌문란” prescribed in Article 91 of the Criminal Act, as the purpose element of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, ultimately means everything that unlawfully destroys the State’s political basic order itself. The political basic order of our country is, needless to say, a liberal democratic political system; therefore, only acts that substantially or formally destroy the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s fundamental freedoms and equality would constitute 국헌문란. Accordingly, the overthrow of a specific government or cabinet, or an act of shouting slogans of overthrow, or whether the means of overthrowing is violence, or the killing of a specific constitutional organ as a natural person and the planning of succession or improvement thereof, would not fall under this.

First, in the case of Defendant A, the Yushin system, by its establishment and continuance alone, was not only an illegal criminal state in which sovereignty was usurped, but its content and operation produced a continuing condition that destroyed the political basic order of a democratic state. Therefore, for Defendant A, the killing of the President, a natural person, was unavoidably done according to a plan long prepared for the restoration of democracy. Even if not so, since after this offense he intended to enact a democratic constitution and organize the National Assembly and Government by democratic methods, there was no purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Second, in the case of Defendant C, it is difficult to conclude, merely because he killed T, the head of the Presidential Security Service, who was not even a state organ established by the Constitution, that he had a purpose of “국헌문란” like the co-defendants; and as to Defendant C, neither his own statement nor his external behavior can be said to show a purpose of “국헌문란.”

Third, in the case of Defendant D, he merely thought that only a few persons would be killed and the President abducted in this offense, and the killing of security officer V and the like, which he admits was done pursuant to the order of his superior, would not amount to 국헌문란. Moreover, Defendant A’s explanation also states that he reached this offense in order to restore liberal democracy, so it cannot be said that there was a purpose to “국헌문란.”

Fourth, in the case of Defendants E, F, and G, the Defendants were merely security guards or drivers of the Central Intelligence Agency restaurant and, having no choice, blindly and mechanically carried out the orders of Defendant D, the chief responsible person there. They could not even imagine the specific harm and consequences. In particular, Defendant G did not know of the murder of the President or even of its plan. Nevertheless, the lower court found, contrary to Defendant C’s explanation, that the facts it held satisfied the purpose of “국헌문란,” and as to the other Defendants, it found that they had carried out riots or killings with the purpose of “국헌문란,” on the ground that they knew a state of national upheaval had occurred. It is argued that this was a fact-finding without evidence (including corroboration required by strict proof), a violation of the rules of evidence contrary to logic and experience, a failure of hearing (especially concerning the specific method after the act), and a defect for lack of reasons (because there were no factual statements that could constitute a purpose to subvert the Constitution); or that the legal principles concerning the purpose of “국헌문란” in the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection were misunderstood. We consider this argument.

(1) First, we examine the legal principles concerning the purpose of “국헌문란.”

Article 91 of the Criminal Act provides: “In this Chapter, ‘purpose of subverting the Constitution’ means any of the following: 1. abolishing the functions of the Constitution or laws without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution or laws; 2. overthrowing, by force, a state organ established by the Constitution or making the exercise of its functions impossible.” Thus it defines “국헌문란.” This ultimately means unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. As argued, it does not necessarily have an extra-legal meaning, and certainly does not mean changing to a communist, monarchical, or dictatorial system. Of course, as argued, killing only a natural person who is a specific state organ, or planning his succession, does not fall under it. Further, since the crime of insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the general principles concerning crimes with specific purpose apply. The purpose belongs to matters requiring strict proof and must be direct, but it cannot be said that it requires a desire or will for the result to occur, nor does it require definite knowledge; a conditional awareness is sufficient (see Supreme Court decision dated April 2, 1968, 68DO61).

(2) Next, we examine the lower court’s factual findings on this point regarding the Defendants.

(A) Part concerning Defendant A

The lower judgment stated the following as the facts of Defendant A’s “purpose of subverting the Constitution”: “While performing his duties as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, Defendant A’s plans for stabilizing the political situation repeatedly failed, exposing his incompetence in carrying out his duties, and after being reprimanded by former President B, rumors of a dismissal for taking responsibility circulated, causing him to feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although he resented the President’s greater trust in T, then head of the Presidential Security Service, who was junior to him and younger, despite T’s arrogant attitude and interference in matters beyond his authority, ... he planned to seize power after killing the President, and, for secrecy, independently devised the concrete plan for the act ... after assassinating the President, he planned to declare martial law on the ground of national security and public disorder, to use the authority and organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency to take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, to constitute a revolutionary committee that would oversee legislative, judicial, and executive powers, to assume the chairmanship himself and secure a basis of power, and then to run for President.” Examining the important basis of this conclusion from the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:

(a) Defendant A’s statements

1) “Q: Why did you call the Army Chief of Staff and ... to the vicinity of the accident site?
A: I lured them from the outset for use after the act; after the act, I would come immediately, keep the Army Chief with me and constantly remain in contact so that he could not entertain other thoughts. When martial law is declared, he will, as martial law commander, handle the situation, so I had called him in advance to sever his contact with the outside and to verify the progress of the situation directly.”
(Same purport in the prosecutor’s record p. 10 and trial transcript pp. 197, 542)

2) “Q: Explain in detail the course of the assassination of the President.
A: ... On the same day, around 16:30, arriving at my office, ... lying down on the bed there, I was for a long time imagining what would happen after the act ... continuing to imagine ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 3-4; trial transcript p. 197 uses the phrase “revolutionary plan”)

3) “Q: Same as above.
A: At around 17:40, after hearing that C, the Chief Secretary of the Blue House, had arrived, I came down to the first floor and entered the reception room. The first words of Chief Secretary C were, ‘The Agency has had a hard time and the Republican Party fellows have ruined everything,’ so I said casually, ‘There is nothing we can do. From now on, when AY’s acting administration is launched, we will have to attach them one by one,’ and ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 4)

4) “Q: Same as above.
A: Sitting again with C on the curb at the right front gate of that entrance, continuing the conversation, after hearing Chief Secretary C say first, ‘That friend T, the chief, is so hard-line and troublesome. He listens only to one or two opposition-party fellows and rushes to report to the President,’ ... I had already resolved to remove the President and T ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 4-5; trial transcript p. 198 to the same effect)

5) “Q: Same as above.
A: ... Then, at around 18:50, the President and T arrived ... and dinner began ... The President asked me, ‘How is the New Democratic Party operation?’ so I said, ‘Because of the Republican Party announcement, everything has been ruined. The fellows who said they would resign have all turned hard-line. As far as I can see, it will be difficult for the AY acting administration system to be launched for the time being. The mainstreams have become hard-line, so it will be somewhat noisy.’”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 5)

6) “Q: But you departed for the Namsan Intelligence Agency. How did you enter Army Headquarters?
A: ... I took Chief Secretary C alone into the adjacent restroom ... and said, ‘You must remove the signboard of the Martial Law Command as soon as possible and change it to the Revolutionary Committee signboard.’”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 17-18)

7) “Then why did you also kill Chief Secretary T?
A: In order for me to carry out the act, I could only achieve the purpose by dealing together with the obstacle T and the escort officers. Also, because T was always manipulating things by hard-line statements and abuse of authority, and frequently frustrated the proposals I made to the President, I removed him together.”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 20-21)

8) “Q: If your purpose was truly pure, could you not have eliminated only the President and then committed suicide on the spot or gone into exile abroad?
A: Only if I survived could I take the initiative over the chaotic political situation after the President’s removal, do the clean-up, and govern according to my plan.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 21)

9) “Q: Were you ever reprimanded by the President?
A: Regarding the recent political and social disorder and efforts to restore order, although I made various proposals as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, it is true that they were not often accepted recently and that I was reprimanded by the President ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 21)

10) “Q: How did you plan the matters after the assassination of the President?
A: ... The content was that after assassinating the President, I would first keep security with Chief Secretary C, who always attended, ... lure military strongmen to the area ... and, after convening an emergency cabinet meeting and declaring nationwide emergency martial law, control the situation by manipulating the Martial Law Commander and gradually transform the Martial Law Command into a Military Revolutionary Committee ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 25-26; trial transcript p. 209 to the same effect)

11) “Q: Same as above.
A: And in order to complete the revolutionary task as quickly as possible, I planned to dissolve the National Assembly, disband the existing political parties, and form a Revolutionary Committee, whose chairman would be me and vice-chairman the Army Chief of Staff, composed only of military officers; and, in order to supervise this, in constituting the Revolutionary Council, I would be chairman, the Prime Minister vice-chairman, and the revolutionary committee members would be the principal Army commanders of the corps level or above, principal Navy commanders of fleet commander level or above, principal Air Force commanders of operations commander level or above, and all ministers at governor level or above, ... Also, the Revolutionary Council would oversee legislation and administration, and as subsidiary organs it would establish under it a Revolutionary Court and Revolutionary Prosecutor’s Office, the latter composed jointly of innovative prosecutors and military prosecutors, and the court would be composed of prominent generals from the military ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 26-27; trial transcript pp. 216, 542 to the same effect)

12) “Q: What is the meaning of revolution?
A: The destruction of the existing order.”
(Trial transcript p. 229)

question: Which of the following statements concerning 압수·수색 are incorrect? (다툼이 있는 경우 pursuant to case law) ㄱ. If the 피압수자 expressly indicated to the 수사기관 that he would not participate in the execution of the 압수·수색영장, then, except in 특별한 사정, it is permissible not to separately guarantee his 변호인 an opportunity to participate in the execution of the 압수·수색영장. ㄴ. If, after the 수사기관 has selectively seized information related to the 범죄 혐의사실 and is retaining the remaining information unrelated thereto without deleting, 폐기, or 반환 it, then, as to the portion unrelated to the 범죄 혐의사실, it has unlawfully 압수 and searched 전자정보 beyond the scope of electronic information subject to seizure without a warrant, and such 위법성 cannot be deemed cured merely because a seizure/search warrant was later issued by a court or because the defendant or defense counsel consented to its use as evidence. ㄷ. The term "an 정보저장매체 belonging to the suspect's ownership or 관리," for which the right of 참여 should be guaranteed not only to the 피압수자 who voluntarily submitted the 정보저장매체 but also to a suspect who is not the voluntary submitter, means a case in which the suspect, at the time of the 압수·수색 or up to a temporally proximate time, actually controlled and 관리 the 정보저장매체 and possessed and exercised exclusive authority to 관리 and dispose of all 전자정보 within that 정보저장매체, and did not otherwise transfer or relinquish it to a third party according to his own intent, so that the suspect can be evaluated as the substantive 피압수자 with respect to the 전자정보 stored in that 정보저장매체. ㄹ. Whether a person qualifies as the substantive 피압수자 must be determined on the basis of the externally and objectively recognizable factual condition at the time of the 압수·수색; thus, if the suspect or any other third party had, in the past, been involved in the use of that 정보저장매체 or the creation or use of individual 전자정보, or if they are the data subject identified by 전자정보 created in the course thereof, then they must be treated as the party substantively subjected to 압수 and 수색. ㅁ. If, while voluntarily submitting a mobile phone, the suspect voluntarily provided the 수사기관 with the ID and password for accessing cloud services or the like, with the intent of submitting to the 수사기관 전자정보 stored not in the mobile phone but in remote locations managed by a third party such as the cloud, then the 전자정보 stored in the cloud or the like may be regarded as having been voluntarily submitted.
