2. Where a prisoner visits with an attorney who is a representative in a litigation case, and where there is no risk of undermining the safety or order of the correctional institution
(5) Except for the matters prescribed in the Act and this Decree, necessary matters concerning the number, time, place, etc. of visits by prisoners other than convicted prisoners, persons sentenced to death, and untried prisoners shall be determined by the Minister of Justice.
(6) If necessary in order to perform affairs concerning the visitation of prisoners by persons outside the correctional institution, the warden may process data containing a resident registration number, passport number, driver’s license number, or alien registration number pursuant to Article 19 of the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act.

Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials amended by Presidential Decree No. 23010 on 2011. 7. 4.
Article 9 Working Hours, etc. (1) The weekly working hours of public officials shall be 40 hours excluding lunch time, and Saturdays shall, in principle, be days off.
(2) The daily working hours of public officials shall be from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and lunch time shall be from 12:00 noon to 1:00 p.m. provided, however, that if the head of an administrative agency deems it necessary in consideration of the nature of the duties, the region, or the special characteristics of the institution, he or she may set lunch time differently within the range of one hour.
(3), (4) Omitted

3. The Claimant’s Arguments
가. The Claimant could not visit suspect 윤○현 because of the Respondents’ denial of visitation in this case, and as a result he lost the opportunity to assist the above suspect, and direct disadvantage was caused to the exercise of the above suspect’s defense rights. The denial of visitation in this case infringed not only the above suspect’s right of access and communication with counsel, but also the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right of access and communication with counsel.
나. Since a detention warrant is sought within 48 hours after a suspect is arrested, the right of a suspect to immediately receive assistance from counsel must be guaranteed during that period as well, and considering that the period immediately before the warrant review hearing is the time when counsel assistance is most needed, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which limits counsel visitation hours to public officials’ working hours, violates the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and infringes the Claimant’s right of access and communication with counsel.
Moreover, where an arrested suspect is housed in a police detention cell, Article 7(1) of the Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc. and Article 37(1) of the Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects apply, so that counsel visitation is permitted even outside the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials. Accordingly, because an unreasonable discrimination arises in the exercise of defense counsel’s right of access and communication depending on whether the suspect is confined in a detention center or housed in a detention cell, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case infringes the Claimant’s right to equality.

4. The Visitation and Communication System between Suspects/Defendants and Defense Counsel
가. Constitutional Basis
The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel. The Constitutional Court has held that even in the case of a suspect who is not detained the right to the assistance of counsel is a natural content recognized under the constitutional principles of a rule-of-law state and due process contained in our Constitution, and Article 12(4) of the Constitution separately and expressly provides for this in order to particularly emphasize the importance of the right to the assistance of counsel for persons under physical restraint see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138. In this manner, a suspect or defendant hereinafter suspect or defendant shall be referred to as suspect, etc. is recognized as having the right to the assistance of counsel regardless of whether he or she is arrested or detained.
In order for a suspect, etc. to sufficiently exercise the right of defense, he or she must be able to consult sufficiently on all factual and legal issues through visitation and communication with defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel hereinafter defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel shall be referred to as defense counsel, etc. With respect to visitation and communication between a suspect, etc. and defense counsel, etc., matters are provided in Article 34 and Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 84(1) and (2), and Article 85 of the Execution of Sentences Act, etc., and these provisions concretize the right to the assistance of counsel guaranteed by the Constitution as above. Among them, Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that a person who intends to become defense counsel also has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc.

나. Meaning of under physical restraint and person who intends to become defense counsel
(1) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint. Here, a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint means not only a suspect, etc. detained pursuant to a detention warrant, but also a suspect, etc. arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant or arrested by emergency arrest or as a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it should be understood to presuppose deprivation of physical liberty in whatever form.
(2) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that not only defense counsel but also a person who intends to become defense counsel has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc. Here, a person who intends to become defense counsel should be understood to include not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment of defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own. It is difficult to say that in a state where physical liberty is suppressed and communication with the outside is severed a suspect, etc. can decide and carry through his or her own intention without being conscious of investigative authorities, and if the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel were permitted only when the suspect, etc. expressly indicates an intention to receive the assistance of counsel, this could result in the existence of the right of visitation and communication being substantially determined by the will of the investigative authorities.
The Supreme Court, in a case where an attorney not appointed as defense counsel expressed an intention to exercise the right of visitation and communication with respect to a suspect arrested, but it was not confirmed what the suspect’s intention was, held that even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.

다. Subject authorized to determine whether to permit visitation
The Execution of Sentences Act aims to promote correction and rehabilitation of convicted prisoners and their sound return to society, and to prescribe matters necessary concerning the treatment and rights of prisoners and the operation of correctional institutions Article 1. Accordingly, Part II of the Execution of Sentences Act regulates the treatment of prisoners, and matters concerning the treatment of prisoners, such as confinement of prisoners, visitation, exchange of correspondence and telephone communication, maintenance of safety and order, discipline and rewards/punishments, and special protection for female prisoners and pregnant women, are vested in the authority of the heads of prisons and detention centers. Meanwhile, the Execution of Sentences Act is a statute that applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required Article 3. In light of the legislative purpose, regulatory content, scope of application, etc. of the Execution of Sentences Act, when there is an application for visitation by a prisoner, this concerns a matter of treatment of prisoners; therefore, if the place is a space where the guarding and control of prisoners by correctional officers is required, it is in principle the warden of the prison or detention center, or the correctional officer entrusted by such warden, who determines whether to permit it.
However, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground, thereby establishing a special provision to the above principle and making the prosecutor or judicial police officer determine whether to permit such visitation when there is an application for visitation by defense counsel during the interrogation of a suspect.
Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, however, regulates the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel and the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel without making any distinction between them; therefore, even where a person who intends to become defense counsel applies for visitation pursuant to Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act during the interrogation of a suspect, the subject who determines whether to permit it should also be the prosecutor or judicial police officer, and such interpretation is consistent with the content of Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act.

5. Determination on Whether the Requirements for Adjudication Are Satisfied
가. Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case
(1) Existence of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case
A constitutional complaint may be filed when fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution are infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act; therefore, in order to file a constitutional complaint, there must first be a fact of exercise or non-exercise of public power that caused the infringement of fundamental rights, and where there is no fact at all of exercise or non-exercise of public power that is subject to constitutional complaint, the petition is unlawful see Constitutional Court 2004. 11. 25. 2004HEONMA178; Constitutional Court 2014. 3. 31. 2014HEONMA239.
Here, as seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor merely informed the correctional officer of the fact that the Claimant had applied for visitation, and even though the Claimant continued to stay in the prosecutor’s office in order to visit suspect 윤○현 after the correctional officer in charge denied visitation between the Claimant and the suspect, the Respondent Prosecutor did not take measures such as allowing the visitation to take place in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room.
Since the Respondent Prosecutor’s failure to take any further measures after the correctional officer’s notice of denial of visitation can be assessed as substantially equivalent to denying the Claimant’s application for visitation see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181; Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28., the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case exists as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint.
(2) Whether the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized - Whether the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel can be regarded as a constitutional fundamental right
가. Organization of the issue
Because the Claimant was not appointed as defense counsel for suspect 윤○현, with respect to the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, only whether the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel was infringed is at issue.
A constitutional complaint is a system by which a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed petitions the Constitutional Court for adjudication in order to obtain relief from that infringement; therefore, for the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case to be lawful, the right allegedly infringed by the Claimant, namely the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel, must not only be recognized as a statutory right but must further be recognized as a constitutional fundamental right.
나. Constitutional Court precedents
The Constitutional Court, in its decision rendered on 2003. 3. 27., 2000HEONMA474, for the first time recognized the core part of the right to assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right, and also took the same position in its decision 2016HEONMA503 rendered on 2017. 11. 30.; the gist of the decision 2016HEONMA503 is as follows.
The right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can be concretely realized in the mutual relationship between them and defense counsel. The right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can become solid through the guarantee of the right of defense counsel to assist them, whereas if the right of defense counsel is not guaranteed, it may become a mere empty shell. The core part of the right of defense counsel to assist a suspect or defendant, without which it becomes a dead letter for them to receive the assistance of counsel, stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel. Therefore, in order to practically secure the right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect and defendant must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.
다. Determination
1) Article 27(4) of the Constitution provides that a criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a conviction becomes final and conclusive, thereby declaring the principle of presumption of innocence. This principle originates from the constitutional ideal that has respect for human dignity as its ultimate goal and seeks to protect the status of suspects, etc., who are in an unfavorable position, so that their disadvantages in criminal proceedings are limited to the minimum necessary. Detention is a system recognized only when there are especially unavoidable reasons with respect to suspects, etc., but the detention system is susceptible to abuse by investigative or trial authorities merely for the convenience of investigation or trial, and while in a detained state, the right to remain silent prescribed in Article 12(2) of the Constitution may not be effectively guaranteed. Accordingly, in order to remove the various harms arising from the situation of physical restraint with respect to suspects, etc. who are presumed innocent and to ensure that detention is not improperly used beyond its original purpose, the main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution guarantees as a fundamental right the right of a person under physical restraint to receive the assistance of counsel as stated above see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONMA144.
The reason for and necessity of recognizing, as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a detained suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel applies equally to arrested suspects, etc.
2) The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution clearly provides that, upon being arrested or detained, a person has the right to prompt assistance of counsel, thereby making clear that suspects, etc. have the right to receive the assistance of counsel even before counsel is appointed. The right of a suspect, etc. who has not yet appointed defense counsel to receive the assistance of counsel is concretized through the appointment of defense counsel; the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel is the starting point and the most basic component of the right to receive the assistance of counsel, and is a right that cannot even be limited by law see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138. Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication with a person who intends to become defense counsel that a suspect, etc. has for purposes of appointing defense counsel must also be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.
3) In order for a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel, a relationship of trust must be formed between the suspect, etc. and the person who intends to become defense counsel, and for this purpose, sufficient consultation must be conducted through visitation and communication with the person who intends to become defense counsel. In this way, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel is intended to solidify the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel and receive assistance from that counsel; if it is not guaranteed, the right of the suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from defense counsel through the appointment of counsel will inevitably become meaningless. Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel is a core part for assisting a suspect, etc., and stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect, etc. to visit and communicate with a person who intends to become defense counsel.
4) Therefore, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel, as a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., must also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right in order to practically secure the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of a person who intends to become defense counsel. Accordingly, this part of the petition seeking a constitutional determination on the ground that the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case infringed the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right, namely the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel, also satisfies the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.
(3) Whether an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is recognized
A constitutional complaint must be filed only after all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act; however, where the claimant failed to take a prior remedy procedure due to a mistake based on justifiable grounds not attributable to his or her disadvantage, or where there is little possibility that the right will be remedied through the prior remedy procedure, or where it is objectively uncertain whether the right-concretization procedure is permitted, making it impossible to expect performance of the prior remedy procedure, it is recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity see Constitutional Court 1989. 9. 4. 88HEONMA22; Constitutional Court 2008. 5. 29. 2007HEONMA712, etc.
However, since the subject who finally determines the Claimant’s application for visitation with suspect 윤○현 is the Respondent Prosecutor, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case falls under dispositions concerning detention by a prosecutor and dispositions concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2 that are subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without first filing a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
The Supreme Court, however, has held that even a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of a denial of visitation by an investigative agency must have a legal interest, and that where the purpose sought to be achieved through the quasi-appeal during the pendency of the case has already been achieved or where the interest has been lost due to the lapse of time or other circumstances, the quasi-appeal becomes unlawful for lack of interest see Supreme Court Decision 98MO121 dated 1999. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2014MO686 dated 2014. 4. 15., yet has not presented specific criteria therefor. Accordingly, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, which ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether the court would deem legal interest to be lacking or would proceed to a merits determination, and thus this is a case where it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure.
Accordingly, this part of the petition should be recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity.
(4) Sub-conclusion
As above, the petition concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case targets an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint, the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is also recognized, and all other requirements for lawfulness are satisfied; thus, it is lawful.

나. The Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case
Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act limits the subject matter of constitutional complaints to acts of public power by providing that a person whose fundamental rights have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint.
According to the record, at the time of the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case, the Respondent Prosecutor handed over the physical custody of suspect 윤○현 to the Respondent Correctional Officer so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but it is recognized that an interrogation of the suspect was scheduled even at night, and thus it may be said that the interrogation of the above suspect was ongoing. In addition, the Claimant at that time applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for counsel visitation.
As seen above, where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect, the prosecutor or judicial police officer must determine whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that a correctional officer who escorted the suspect to the investigative agency is not vested with the authority to permit or restrict such visitation.
Article 118 of the Operational Guidelines on the Management of Prisoners Ministerial Instruction of the Ministry of Justice No. 1077, 2015. 1. 13., which was in force at the time of this case, provided that where there is an application for defense counsel visitation with a prisoner outside the institution who is being escorted out, the escorting correctional officer is to conduct the visitation between the escorted prisoner and defense counsel through certain procedures, such as obtaining permission from the warden. However, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center, or a correctional officer delegated by them, determines whether to permit it, and cannot be said to apply to cases, such as this one, where an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. is made during the interrogation of a suspect, and the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it.
Ultimately, in this case, because it cannot be said that the Respondent Correctional Officer had the authority to determine whether to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect 윤○현, the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case does not constitute an exercise of public power that is made subject to constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act.

다. The Visitation Hours Provision in this case
The main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court, which means that only a person whose own fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been currently and directly infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint. Therefore, if the exercise of public power has no effect whatsoever on the legal status of the person seeking to file a constitutional complaint, then there is no possibility or danger of infringement of fundamental rights in the first place, and filing a constitutional complaint against such exercise of public power is not permitted see Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA368; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2012HEONMA630, etc.
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case is a provision that applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and it cannot be said to apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that the denial or restriction of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect cannot be based on that provision. In practice as well, the police and prosecutors impose no time restrictions whatsoever on visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect see Article 7 of the Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc., Article 37(2) of the Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects, Article 2(6) and Article 8 of the Guidelines on the Operation of Defense Counsel Participation in Suspect Interrogation, and Article 230 of the Guidelines on Defense Counsel Visitation and Communication with Suspects.
As seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation with suspect 윤○현, against whom interrogation was continuing, and therefore the Visitation Hours Provision in this case does not apply here, nor did the Respondent Prosecutor at the time deny the above visitation application by applying that provision. Accordingly, this part of the petition lacks self-relatedness for purposes of the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.

6. Determination on Whether the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in This Case Infringed Fundamental Rights
가. Whether the Claimant’s right of access and communication was restricted
As seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation and remained in the prosecutor’s office, but due to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ultimately could not visit suspect 윤○현 and left the prosecutor’s office; accordingly, it is reasonable to view the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as having restricted the Claimant’s right of access and communication with the above suspect.
However, according to the record, suspect 윤○현 did not raise an objection to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, visited with another attorney twice the following day, and that attorney personally appeared and responded at the pre-detention suspect interrogation hearing. Nevertheless, even if the suspect did not indicate an intention to visit and communicate with a person who intends to become defense counsel, if a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, visitation with the suspect must be permitted see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.; moreover, the Claimant had even been entrusted by suspect 윤○현’s family and intended to visit the suspect, so at the time of the visitation application there was sufficient possibility that the Claimant would become defense counsel for the above suspect; and the person claiming infringement of fundamental rights caused by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is not suspect 윤○현 but the Claimant. In light of these circumstances, the facts recognized above are not factors to be considered in determining whether the Claimant’s fundamental rights were infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case.

나. Whether the Claimant’s visitation application was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication
Because the right of access and communication of defense counsel, etc. must be exercised within the limits that do not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system, attempts by defense counsel, etc. to visit a suspect, etc. beyond the limits that can realistically be guaranteed in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances do not constitute a proper exercise of the right of access and communication and cannot be permitted see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO657 dated 2007. 1. 31.; Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.
However, in this case, since suspect 윤○현 was scheduled to continue being interrogated at night on that day, it appears that measures could have been taken to permit visitation and communication between the Claimant and the above suspect in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room before the interrogation, and thus in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances at the time of the visitation application, no specific circumstances are discernible showing that the Claimant, who intended to become defense counsel, attempted to abuse the exercise of visitation and communication with the suspect beyond the limits realistically guaranteeable or beyond the original purpose of the physical restraint system.
Accordingly, the Claimant’s visitation application must be deemed to have been exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a person who intends to become defense counsel.

다. Whether it was based on the Constitution or statutes
(1) In the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc., free visitation, that is, visitation in which confidentiality regarding the content of the conversation is fully guaranteed and the parties may converse freely without any restriction, influence, pressure, or improper interference, is not of a nature that can be restricted under any pretext see Constitutional Court 1992. 1. 28. 91HEONMA111. However, this means only that such is the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc.; it does not mean that no restriction whatsoever may be imposed on visitation itself with defense counsel, etc. The right to the assistance of counsel and the right of visitation and communication with counsel, which is one component thereof, may, like all other constitutional fundamental rights, be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26. 2009HEONMA341; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2015HEONMA243, and the same shall apply to the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel.
(2) As seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor temporarily handed over the physical custody of suspect 윤○현 to the correctional officer in charge so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but since a night interrogation of the above suspect was planned, it may be said that the investigation or interrogation of the above suspect was continuing.
Although the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel, etc. may be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law, neither the Constitution nor laws such as the Criminal Procedure Act contain a provision allowing restriction or refusal where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect. This is to ensure, in light of the importance of the right of access and communication held by a suspect, etc., that the right of access and communication held by defense counsel, etc. is also guaranteed to the maximum extent.
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which is delegated by Article 41(4) of the Execution of Sentences Act, restricts visitation and communication between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. by limiting visitation by prisoners to working hours pursuant to the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials; however, as seen above, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and does not apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it, and thus it must be said that visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. cannot be denied or restricted on the basis of that provision.
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes.

라. Sub-conclusion
Ultimately, the Claimant’s visitation application concerning suspect 윤○현 was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a person who intends to become defense counsel, and furthermore the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes; therefore, it infringed the Claimant’s right of access and communication.

7. Conclusion
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case should be found unconstitutional and revoked; however, since the denial of visitation has already ended, we shall, for declaratory purposes and to prevent repetition of the same or similar infringement of fundamental rights, make a determination that it is unconstitutional. The petition regarding the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case and the Visitation Hours Provision in this case is unlawful in its entirety and shall therefore be dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the order. The concurrence of the remaining participating Justices was reached, except for the dissenting opinion by Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as stated in Section 8 below.

8. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok on the Prosecutor’s Denial of Visitation in This Case
We are of the view that the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also unlawful and should be dismissed, and we state our opinion as follows.

가. Possibility of Infringement of Fundamental Rights
(1) A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power. Therefore, a constitutional complaint alleging infringement of a right based merely on statute, rather than on a constitutional fundamental right, is unlawful.
(2) In the Constitutional Court’s decision 2012HEONMA610 rendered on 2015. 7. 30., three Justices presented the following separate opinion.
The right to the assistance of counsel means sufficiently and substantively guaranteeing the activities of defense counsel aimed at assisting the person arrested, etc. Thus, the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes, as concrete means for substantively guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel, the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel Article 34, defense counsel’s right to inspect and copy investigative and litigation records Articles 35 and 266-3, and defense counsel’s right to participate in various procedures such as investigation and trial Articles 121, 163, 243-2, etc.
The reason special rights such as the right to inspect and copy records or the right of visitation and communication are recognized for defense counsel is that they all originate from the purpose of faithfully guaranteeing the right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel, and it cannot be viewed as a right recognized in order to guarantee defense counsel’s own fundamental rights. Defense counsel exercises the right to assist as defense counsel recognized in the Criminal Procedure Act for the benefit of the person arrested, etc. as an assistant to the person arrested, etc., not for the protection of his or her own fundamental rights. Therefore, the right to assist as defense counsel should be viewed as a statutory right recognized as a result of the legislator concretely shaping it through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act in order to faithfully guarantee the constitutional fundamental right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel.
From this perspective, the Constitutional Court has long held that the constitutional right of visitation and communication with defense counsel is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects and defendants, and that defense counsel’s own right of visitation and communication with a suspect or defendant cannot be regarded as a constitutional right, but is merely a right guaranteed only by Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act; accordingly, it dismissed a constitutional complaint filed by defense counsel on the ground that there was no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181.
For the reasons stated in the above separate opinion, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel is also merely a statutory right specifically formed through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act as an indirect and incidental effect arising from recognizing the right to receive the assistance of counsel of a person arrested, etc. as a fundamental right, and cannot be viewed as an independent fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.
(3) The majority opinion relies on the Court’s majority opinions in Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA474 decided on 2003. 3. 27. and Constitutional Court 2016HEONMA503 decided on 2017. 11. 30., which held that in order for the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel to be practically secured, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, and reasons that the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel should also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right because it is a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., and if it is not guaranteed, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless.
It is true that through visitation counsel can grasp the status of a detained suspect, etc. and devise appropriate responses accordingly, explain the meaning of the facts of suspicion or the charges, consult about countermeasures by hearing the opinions of the suspect, etc. thereon, and provide comfort to a suspect, etc. who is in a legally and psychologically anxious state, thereby restoring psychological stability and enabling the suspect, etc. to effectively exercise the right of defense within the criminal procedure see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992. It is also true that through visitation and communication between a person who intends to become defense counsel and a suspect, etc., such advice, consultation, and comfort to the suspect, etc. are possible to some extent. However, when a person who intends to become defense counsel visits and communicates with a suspect, etc., because the point at which it is confirmed whether the suspect, etc. will actually retain the attorney and receive assistance from him or her has not yet been reached, the main purpose may be seen as the person’s own retention activities rather than assistance to the suspect, etc.; and the disadvantage suffered by the person who intends to become defense counsel due to inability to visit the suspect, etc., namely the disadvantage resulting from failure to obtain a criminal case retention, is merely an indirect, factual, and economic interest see Constitutional Court 2004. 4. 29. 2002HEONMA756.
Meanwhile, as stated by the majority opinion, it is reasonable to view not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment as defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own, as falling within the meaning of a person who intends to become defense counsel, and the Supreme Court has also held that even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9. If the meaning of a person who intends to become defense counsel is interpreted as above, the right of visitation and communication of such a person should be viewed as a right recognized to that person regardless of the suspect’s or defendant’s will, at the stage before assisting the suspect, etc.
In light of the above circumstances, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel cannot be viewed as standing in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the right of a suspect, etc. to receive assistance, and it cannot be concluded that, unless it is elevated and guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless. Therefore, even if one adopts the view that the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist a suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, there is no need, as in the majority opinion, to understand the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel as well as a constitutional fundamental right.
(4) Ultimately, the right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel, which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be regarded as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution; accordingly, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint against the denial of visitation is unlawful because there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.

나. Subsidiarity
(1) Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that if there is an objection to a disposition concerning detention, seizure, or the return of seized articles made by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, or to a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2, a petition may be filed with the court having jurisdiction over the place where the duties are performed, or with the court corresponding to the prosecutor’s public prosecutors’ office to which the prosecutor belongs, for revocation or alteration of the disposition.
An act by an investigative agency denying visitation between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. falls under a disposition concerning detention or a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore not only the suspect or defense counsel but also a person who intends to become defense counsel may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal pursuant to that provision see Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO656 dated 2007. 1. 31., etc.
A constitutional complaint may not be filed unless all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act, and the Constitutional Court has held that where a constitutional complaint is filed without going through such a procedure despite the availability of a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is unlawful for failure to exhaust the lawful remedy procedure prescribed by other laws see Constitutional Court 2007. 5. 31. 2006HEONMA1131.
(2) The Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case constitutes a disposition concerning detention or a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. subject to a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without seeking revocation or alteration of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case through the quasi-appeal procedure.
The majority opinion held that, because the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ended on the day of the incident, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation thereof, it would be objectively uncertain whether the court would proceed to a merits determination, and thus it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure; on that basis, it concluded that the constitutional complaint concerning the denial of visitation was lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.
However, after the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, the Claimant was unable to visit suspect 윤○현 or participate in the interrogation of the suspect, and ultimately was not retained as defense counsel for the above suspect. In addition, with respect to the above suspect, a detention warrant was issued and he was prosecuted while in custody. There is nothing in the record to suggest any circumstance that would lead a court to find legal interest to be lacking or extinguished if the Claimant filed a quasi-appeal against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case. The Supreme Court has decided on the merits on the premise that legal interest exists even when defense counsel’s participation was denied during the interrogation of a suspect and the interrogation procedure had ended see Supreme Court Decision 2008MO793 dated 2008. 9. 12.; the same should apply where visitation is denied during the interrogation of a suspect.
Accordingly, even if the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case has already ended, the Claimant may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act; thus, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint regarding the denial of visitation in this case fails to satisfy the subsidiarity requirement and is unlawful.

다. Conclusion
The right of visitation and communication of a person who intends to become defense counsel, which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be said to be a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and therefore the Claimant’s petition regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case lacks the possibility of infringement of a fundamental right. Moreover, because the Claimant did not go through the quasi-appeal procedure under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the subsidiarity requirement is also not satisfied.
Accordingly, the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is unlawful in any event and must be dismissed."}

Subject Matter of Review\\n\\nThe subject matter of this case is whether Article 63(1) of the Immigration Control Act, as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18., hereinafter the provision subject to review, violates the Constitution. The term detention means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under any item of Article 46(1) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act, as amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.\\n\\nArticle 46 (Persons Subject to Deportation) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may deport outside the Republic of Korea an alien falling under any of the following items in accordance with the procedures prescribed in this Chapter.\\n\\n2. An alien who has violated Article 7-2 or an alien who entered the Republic of Korea through acts such as fraudulent invitation prescribed in that Article\\n\\n3. A person whose ground for denial of entry, falling under any item of Article 11(1), is discovered or arises after entry\\n\\n8. A person who has violated Article 17(1) or (2), Article 18, Article 20, Article 23, Article 24, or Article 25\\n\\nArticle 63 (Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Subject to a Deportation Order) (2) Where the period of detention under paragraph (1) exceeds 3 months, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office shall obtain prior approval from the Minister of Justice every 3 months.\\n\\n(3) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office shall promptly release a person from detention if prior approval under paragraph (2) is not obtained.\\n\\n(4) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may release a person from detention if it becomes manifest that the person subject to a deportation order cannot be repatriated for reasons such as denial of entry from another country.\\n\\n(5) Where the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office releases a person from detention pursuant to paragraph (3) or (4), he or she may attach restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions.\\n\\nArticle 66 (Revocation of Temporary Release from Detention) (1) Where a person temporarily released from detention falls under any of the following items, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may revoke the temporary release from detention and take measures for detention again.\\n\\n1. Where the person violates conditions attached to the temporary release, other than the matters prescribed in Items 1 and 2\\n\\n(2) Where the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office revokes the temporary release from detention pursuant to paragraph (1), he or she may issue a revocation document of temporary release from detention and forfeit all or part of the security deposit to the National Treasury.\\n\\nImmigration Control Act, as amended by Act No. 15492 on 2018. 3. 20.\\n\\nArticle 65 (Temporary Release from Detention) (1) The head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee including his or her surety or legal representative, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters.\\n\\n3. Grounds for the Referring Court’s Request for Constitutional Review\\n\\nA. The provision subject to review does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby rendering the detainee unable to predict at all when he or she will be released, which itself causes serious mental pressure. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of facilitating execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and thus violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person.\\n\\nB. Detention under the Immigration Control Act restricts freedom of the person as it is equivalent to arrest or detention in criminal procedure. Therefore, it should be subject to a strict warrant principle; yet the provision subject to review allows the physical restraint of an alien subject to a deportation order without a court warrant, and thus violates the warrant principle.\\n\\nC. In light of the fact that no third independent and neutral institution or judicial body is involved at all in the stage of commencement or extension of detention; that the detainee may file an objection against the detention order with the Minister of Justice, and detention may be extended only with the Minister of Justice’s approval, but the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency that issues and executes detention orders, so it cannot be said that ex post remedies or control procedures by an external neutral and objective institution are secured; and that there is no provision in the Immigration Control Act requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to present opinions before issuance of a detention order under the provision subject to review, the provision subject to review violates the principle of due process.\\n\\n4. Judgment\\n\\nA. Alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act\\n\\n(1) Detention under the Immigration Control Act means enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under Article 46(1) of the Immigration Control Act in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person. Detention under the Immigration Control Act includes detention for the determination of a person subject to deportation prescribed in Article 51 and detention for the execution of a deportation order prescribed in the provision subject to review.\\n\\n(2) According to the provision subject to review, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain an alien subject to a deportation order, hereinafter a person subject to deportation, in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, hereinafter a detention facility, until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation. Detention under the provision subject to review is intended to secure the execution of a deportation order where a deportation order has been issued upon determining that an alien falls under a person subject to deportation, but immediate execution is impossible, and is distinguished from detention under Article 51 of the Immigration Control Act, which secures the physical presence of an alien in order to examine whether the alien falls under a person subject to deportation.\\n\\nThe provision subject to review states that detention is permissible until such person can be repatriated, and thus, in the wording of the statute, imposes no limitation on the detention period; instead, where the period of detention exceeds 3 months, prior approval from the Minister of Justice must be obtained every 3 months, and if such approval is not obtained, detention must be released. In addition, a person detained in a detention facility pursuant to the provision subject to review may file an objection with the Minister of Justice, and the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters.\\n\\nB. Issues and Standard of Review\\n\\n(1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure by which a person subject to deportation is taken and confined in a detention facility in order to secure execution of a deportation order when immediate execution of the deportation order is impossible, and thus restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person by violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which is the limiting principle on restriction of fundamental rights, and the principle of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution.\\n\\n(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that promotes the national interest and security by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry and exit of nationals and foreigners and the stay of foreigners. Among matters relating to immigration control, matters concerning the entry and domestic stay of foreigners are necessary for performing the functions of a sovereign state and lie within the domain of broad policy discretion. Detention under the provision subject to review, which is carried out to secure execution of a deportation order, may be regarded as part of immigration control administration.\\n\\nHowever, freedom of the person under Article 12(1) of the Constitution is the most fundamental minimum freedom necessary to realize human dignity and value, and serves as the premise for the guarantee of all fundamental rights. By its nature, it is a human right, and whether it is recognized does not vary depending on whether one has lawful status of stay in the country. Therefore, a strict standard of review must be applied to whether the provision subject to review infringes freedom of the person.\\n\\nC. Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon\\n\\n(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated\\n\\n(a) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means\\n\\nThe legislative purpose of the provision subject to review is to appropriately control and adjust the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners, thereby promoting national security and order, by taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea so that deportation orders may be executed easily and efficiently. Such legislative purpose is legitimate, and taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea is an effective means of securing execution of a deportation order; thus, appropriateness of means is also recognized.\\n\\n(b) Minimum infringement and balance of interests\\n\\nHowever, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the minimum infringement requirement and the balance of interests requirement for the following reasons.\\n\\n1) Detention under the provision subject to review is a compulsory measure temporarily and provisionally taken to secure execution when a deportation order cannot be executed immediately upon issuance. Yet the provision subject to review merely provides that a person subject to deportation may be detained until such person can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby making indefinite detention possible.\\n\\nDetention by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily and provisionally confined in a specific place for the purpose of executing a deportation order can, by its very nature, be deemed justified only when the person is confined within a reasonable period necessary for the execution of the deportation order. However, according to the provision subject to review, for example, where the detainee has applied for refugee status recognition under the Refugee Act or has filed an objection to a decision of non-recognition of refugee status, etc., so that the deportation order cannot be executed until the related procedures are completed, or where the detainee has filed an action for cancellation, etc. against the deportation order or civil or criminal disputes are pending, making execution of the deportation order practically difficult, the detention period may be extended indefinitely depending on the progress of those procedures. Long-term or indefinite detention of a person subject to deportation even where the deportation order cannot be executed within a considerable period exceeds the limits of a temporary and provisional compulsory measure and seriously restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Furthermore, detention without an upper limit on duration causes serious mental pressure in itself, regardless of the actual length of detention, because the detainee cannot predict at all when he or she will be released.\\n\\nDetention under the provision subject to review has a substantive limitation in purpose, in that it may not be ordered for any purpose other than securing execution of a deportation order; and it has a temporal limitation in that it may be temporary only for the minimum period necessary until repatriation is possible and the period of detention may not be extended for other purposes. Although the average detention period until an actual person subject to deportation is repatriated is only a little over 10 days, and cases in which long-term detention exceeding one year becomes an issue are only few, such limitations naturally derive from the nature of detention as a temporary and provisional measure. Therefore, notwithstanding the above interpretive limitations, the provision subject to review, which does not set an upper limit on detention period, still leaves unresolved the problems arising from the absence of such an upper limit, in that long-term or indefinite detention is possible.\\n\\nMeanwhile, there may be cases where there is no objective reason making repatriation impossible, but the detainee does not cooperate with repatriation, making it impossible to execute the deportation order promptly; however, non-cooperation with repatriation alone cannot justify indefinite detention.\\n\\n2) Therefore, even if the appropriate upper limit on the detention period is left aside, at the very least the law must clearly specify that upper limit so as to prevent harm arising from unreasonable prolongation or uncertainty of the detention period. Permitting detention without a time limit merely for the administrative purpose of efficient execution of a deportation order emphasizes only administrative convenience and uniformity, and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. It is difficult to regard foreigners who were not able to choose voluntary departure for various reasons or who were unable to depart voluntarily and therefore were apprehended and detained as having, in effect, a freedom to depart, so the infringement of fundamental rights due to the absence of an upper limit on detention period cannot be deemed mitigated on that ground.\\n\\nLooking to international standards and foreign legislation, many countries set an upper limit on the period when detaining a person subject to a deportation order. The EU Returns Directive, Directive 2008/115/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on common standards and procedures in Member States for returning illegally staying third-country nationals, requires Member States to prescribe in domestic law an absolute maximum period of detention in order to curb unnecessary long-term detention and respect the basic human rights of foreigners subject to deportation. Accordingly, EU Member States have enacted domestic laws establishing detention requirements and procedures that are equal to or stricter than the standards set forth in the directive and have set upper limits on detention periods. For example, France provides by law that detention may be ordered up to a maximum of 90 days only where effective custody is difficult and other measures are insufficient. Germany provides by law that detention for deportation may be ordered up to 6 months, but even upon extension may not exceed a maximum of 12 months. Taiwan and South Africa also limit by statute the detention period for persons subject to deportation to a maximum of 100 days or 120 days, respectively.\\n\\n3) If an upper limit is set on the detention period, and repatriation is delayed so that the period exceeds that upper limit, detention of the person subject to deportation must be released. In such a case, it may be argued that the person subject to deportation who has been released may go into hiding or be exposed to crime. However, this is merely a vague and potential possibility that has not yet materialized, and a concern that exaggerates some situations; thus, based only on such vague assumptions, it is difficult to justify measures that seriously restrict freedom of the person, such as detention without any upper limit on duration.\\n\\nThere may be concern that if an upper limit is imposed, the detainee could exceed that upper limit through a cancellation action or by applying for refugee status recognition, etc.; however, such cases can be minimized through institutional improvements such as having the courts give priority and focus to such cases, expediting refugee status examination and decisions, or preventing abuse of refugee status applications.\\n\\nFurthermore, securing execution of a deportation order is possible through various means other than detention under the provision subject to review, such as restricting the residence of a person subject to deportation until departure requirements are met, requiring periodic reporting of residence, designating a guarantor or requiring payment of an appropriate security deposit, or continuously observing or supervising the person subject to deportation through supervisors, etc. Therefore, in order to secure execution of a deportation order, it is not inevitable to adopt a method that excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person, such as detention without an upper limit on duration.\\n\\n4) Meanwhile, the current procedures and operation of the Immigration Control Act are insufficient, by themselves, to properly control the detention period and thereby mitigate excessive restrictions on freedom of the person. The temporary release from detention system and the approval system for extension of detention periods exist, but they are largely left to the discretion of the same administrative authority that issues and executes detention orders, and the statistics also show that the effectiveness of those systems is limited.\\n\\n5) Taking the above circumstances together, although means exist for securing execution of a deportation order other than indefinite detention in a detention facility, the provision subject to review allows the detainee to be detained without any upper limit on duration, which exceeds the minimum necessary to achieve the legislative purpose and excessively restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person. Even if the public interest sought is important, the degree of restriction is too great; therefore, the provision subject to review fails to satisfy the requirements of minimum infringement and balance of interests.\\n\\n(c) Conclusion\\n\\nThe provision subject to review infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person in violation of the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction.\\n\\n(2) Whether the principle of due process is violated\\n\\n(a) Article 12(1) of the Constitution declares the principle of due process by providing that no person shall be punished, placed under preventive restrictions, or subjected to forced labor, except by virtue of law and due process. The principle of due process is not limited to criminal procedure but applies to all state action generally. Therefore, the constitutional principle of due process must also be observed in detention under the provision subject to review.\\n\\n(b) When freedom of the person is restricted by coercive measures in administrative procedure, control by a neutral institution independent from the executing agency is an important component of due process. Considering that detention under the provision subject to review seeks to secure execution of a deportation order and restricts freedom of the person to the extent of deprivation, an institution independent from and neutral to the immigration control official must be able to review and control the validity of detention at the stage of commencement or extension of detention. However, under the current system, no independent neutral institution at all is involved at the stage of commencement or extension of detention, and in substance the detention decision-making body and the executing body cannot be said to be separated.\\n\\nThe detainee may file an objection with the Minister of Justice against the detention order, and prior approval by the Minister of Justice is required when the detention period exceeds 3 months; however, the Minister of Justice is merely the supervisory authority over the administrative agency issuing and executing detention orders, so this cannot be regarded as securing a review system by an external neutral and objective institution. The reality that a detention order is almost automatically issued once a deportation order exists, and that extension approval is almost always granted, also shows this.\\n\\n(c) Providing the parties with an opportunity to submit opinions and materials is an important procedural requirement derived from due process. However, the Immigration Control Act does not contain any provision requiring that the person concerned be given an opportunity to submit opinions before a detention order is issued pursuant to the provision subject to review. The Administrative Procedures Act excludes dispositions concerning the entry and departure of foreigners from its scope, so under current law the detainee is not given an opportunity to make statements or submit opinions favorable to him or her in the detention order procedure. An objection to detention, even though it exists, is only discretionary ex post control by the Minister of Justice and does not amount to a judicial-like neutral review.\\n\\n(d) Taken together, the provision subject to review violates the constitutional principle of due process because there is no control procedure by a fair and neutral institution at the stage of commencement or extension of detention and because the person concerned is not guaranteed an opportunity to submit opinions.\\n\\n(3) Necessity of a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution and temporary application\\n\\nAs examined above, the provision subject to review violates the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction and the principle of due process and thereby infringes the detainee’s freedom of the person; therefore, as a matter of principle, a simple declaration of unconstitutionality would be appropriate. However, because the unconstitutionality lies in the absence of an upper limit on detention period and the absence of meaningful neutral control and opportunity to submit opinions, a simple declaration would create an intolerable legal vacuum concerning detention for execution of deportation orders. Accordingly, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered, and continued application shall be ordered until the legislature enacts remedial legislation by no later than 2025. 5. 31. If no remedial legislation is enacted by then, the provision subject to review shall lose effect from 2025. 6. 1.\\n\\nD. Constitutional Opinion of Justice Lee Seon-ae\\n\\nI concur with the conclusion that the provision subject to review violates the Constitution and that a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution should be rendered. However, I have already participated in and argued in the dissenting opinion in Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29, so I cite that reasoning and leave my dissenting opinion in this case. The reasoning leading to a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution is the same as the constitutional opinion above.\\n\\n5. Conclusion\\n\\nSince the provision subject to review is not in conformity with the Constitution, a decision of incompatibility with the Constitution shall be rendered, and the provision shall be provisionally applied until remedial legislation by the legislature is enacted, with 2025. 5. 31. as the deadline. In addition, Constitutional Court Decision 2017HEONGA29, in which the Court had previously held a different view, shall be modified to the extent inconsistent with this decision. Except for the dissenting opinions of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin, the opinions of the Justices participating in this decision were unanimous.\\n\\n6. Dissenting Opinion of Justices Lee Eun-ae, Lee Jong-seok, and Lee Yeong-jin\\n\\nWe conclude that the provision subject to review does not violate the Constitution. The precedent of the Constitutional Court, the need to recognize a change of precedent, the continuity of institutional improvement in practice, the difficulty of imposing a fixed upper limit on detention in the immigration context, and the sufficiency of alternative release and objection procedures all support the view that the provision subject to review remains constitutional.\\n\\n7. Supplementary Opinion of Justice Lee Mi-seon\\n\\nIn addition to the constitutional opinion of the five Justices, I state that the provision subject to review also violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution, which provides the right to request judicial review of the legality of arrest or detention. The constitutional guarantee of 체포·구속적부심사 extends broadly to all public-power restrictions on freedom of the person, including administrative detention. Because the current Immigration Control Act does not establish a procedure by which the legality of the commencement or continuation of detention under the provision subject to review may be requested to a court for review, and because the Habeas Corpus Act excludes persons detained pursuant to the Immigration Control Act, foreigners detained under the provision subject to review are left without a court-based remedy on the detention itself. Ex post administrative objections or approval procedures by the Minister of Justice cannot substitute for judicial review. Therefore, the provision subject to review violates Article 12(6) of the Constitution."}
